subtopic: ST. LAWRENCE RIVER EAST OF MONTREAL   SUGGESTED USE OF ICEBREAKERS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, before you proceed with the orders of the day, I have an extremely important and urgent question to address to the Minister of Transport in my capacity as member for the most highly industrialized county in the province of Quebec.
Is the Minister of Transport aware that the St. Lawrence river, as is the case nearly every year, is now flooding the east end of the island of Montreal and has wrought considerable damage in my county? Does the government intend to do something to cope with that condition?
In order to prevent such disasters in the future, may I suggest that the government should dispatch to that part of the river, each spring, two icebreakers at least in order to break the ice-jam at the onset.

subtopic: ST. LAWRENCE RIVER EAST OF MONTREAL   SUGGESTED USE OF ICEBREAKERS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I wish to thank the hon. member for having given me notice of his question. I may assure him that the Department of Transport is aware of the damages caused by the swelling of the St. Lawrence river at Montreal. As soon as that condition was brought to our attention we immediately dispatched three icebreakers to the scene. The Ernest Lapointe, the Saurel and the Lady Grey are now breaking the ice and according to the latest reports I have received the situation is improving considerably.
The hon. member may rest assured that the suggestion he made in the last part of his question will be taken into consideration by the government.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO REVOCATION OF CITIZENSHIP, ETC.
speechtext: Explain.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO REVOCATION OF CITIZENSHIP, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as forecast in the speech from the throne, it is proposed in this bill to amend the Canadian Citizenship Act to prevent the retention of Canadian citizenship by persons who have renounced their allegiance or shown by their conduct that they are not loyal to Canada.
It is not a lengthy bill; in fact it contains but one section amending certain parts of section 19 of the present act.
Under the Naturalization Act, which was repealed with the coming into force of the Canadian Citizenship Act on January 1, 1947, there was provision, under subsection 1 of section 9 thereof, for the revocation of a certificate of naturalization by the governor in council after the minister was satisfied that the person to whom the certificate was granted had shown himself, by act or speech, to be disaffected or disloyal to His Majesty. This provision was applicable whether the offence was committed in Canada or outside of Canada.
When the Canadian Citizenship Act was being considered, it was decided to make the citizenship of a Canadian citizen, other than a natural-born Canadian citizen, liable to revocation only if the offence of disaffection or disloyalty had been committed outside of Canada, and to make it applicable in Canada only in the event of the naturalized Canadian citizen having been convicted of treason or sedition by a court of competent jurisdiction. These persons had the right to have their

cases considered by a commission, appointed under section 19 of the act. In this way their right to have a hearing was fully protected.
In recent years it has been found that a number of naturalized Canadian citizens have returned to the countries of their origin with the obvious intention of remaining there permanently and of severing their allegiance to Canada. Under present legislation, their citizenship can be revoked only after a period of not less than six years' residence outside of Canada and failure to maintain substantial connection with Canada.
In some cases a number of naturalized persons have asked, while still in Canada, to have their certificates of naturalization or citizenship cancelled on the ground that they no longer wish to retain Canadian citizenship. There is nothing in the present legislation covering this type of disaffection.
So far my remarks have had reference to the revocation of the citizenship of persons other than natural-born Canadian citizens. At present a Canadian citizen by birth loses his citizenship only on the voluntary acquisition of a foreign nationality. Very serious thought, however, has been given to the question of the revocation of the citizenship of persons, whether naturalized or natural-born, who take an oath or make an affirmation or other formal declaration of allegiance to a foreign state, whether they were residing in or out of Canada at the time of taking such action.
In view of the conditions which I have stated, and for obvious reasons of security, it is deemed desirable to introduce certain new grounds for revocation of citizenship.
Under present legislation, revocation may take place only if the naturalized Canadian citizen has been residing outside of Canada for a period of not less than six years and has failed to maintain substantial connection with Canada. The proposed amendment provides for revocation after a residence of two years in a country of which the Canadian citizen was a national or citizen at any time prior to his becoming a Canadian citizen or being naturalized in Canada. This would allow more speedy disposition of cases where naturalized persons return to their country of origin and lose substantial connection with Canada.
There is, further, an extension of the present provision for revocation for disloyalty. At present, revocation is possible where a person out of Canada shows himself "by act or speech" to be "disaffected or disloyal" to His Majesty or, if in Canada, is guilty of treason or sedition. The latter phraseology, especially, is too narrow. It does not, for instance, cover persons convicted of offences
Canadian Citizenship Act under the Official Secrets Act. It is proposed in this amendment to allow revocation for disaffection and disloyalty out of Canada, and for persons in Canada who are found guilty of sedition, espionage, treason or similar offences.
Subsection 3 of section 1 of the bill provides for the revocation of the citizenship of all categories of citizens whether naturalized or natural-born.
There is no substantial change in paragraph (a) from the present legislation, which provides for the revocation of the citizenship of a person who, by a voluntary and formal act other than marriage, acquires the nationality or citizenship of a foreign country, whilst in Canada.
Paragraph (b) of subsection 3 is new. It provides for revocation in the case of persons who take an oath or make an affirmation or other formal declaration of allegiance to a foreign state; this would apply whether the persons were in or out of Canada.
There is, finally, provision in paragraph
(c)	of subsection 3 for the revocation of the citizenship of those persons who make declarations renouncing their Canadian citizenship. This amendment would have the effect of legalizing the action of a person who renounces his Canadian citizenship, whether in or out of Canada.
The government is of the opinion that the amendments to the Canadian Citizenship Act which are proposed in this bill are essential to the welfare and security of Canada. I wish to make it clear, however, that the rights of any person, the revocation of whose citizenship might be considered under any one of these proposed amendments, are fully protected under that part of section 19 of the citizenship act which provides, upon request, for a formal hearing by a commission constituted for the purpose by the governor in council. It is not proposed in this bill to deprive a person of his citizenship without granting him his right to have his case considered by this tribunal.

speakeroldname: Mr. George A. Drew (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO REVOCATION OF CITIZENSHIP, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this bill, so far as it goes, makes it possible to deal with certain acts of disloyalty, but it does not deal effectively with many of the things that are being done by people who have come to Canada, have become naturalized Canadians and are now abusing the rights of that citizenship in an effort to undermine our democratic system. I shall support the bill before the house because the terms are good so far as they go. It is appropriate, however, in dealing with the principle now under consideration, to point out the advantage of going a great deal further; because the
1572	HOUSE OF
Canadian Citizenship Act government itself could put forward appropriate amendments, if they were considered advisable, to carry the application of the bill to a wider field.
As has been pointed out by the minister, a number of people who have come to Canada have become naturalized and have then returned to their own country with the apparent intention of staying there. I am not objecting to their loss of citizenship. I should think that under those circumstances the loss of citizenship would be almost automatic. There is, however, a consideration that should be borne in mind. Some of those very people are now returning to Canada more completely disillusioned about communism-and we know it is communism that is under consideration-than anyone else in this country. I suggest that we should not disregard the possibility that some of the most effective exponents of our free democracy may be those who have mistakenly returned to the slave states and have seen what is actually going on there at the present time. That, however, is an observation that would apply only to a limited number. I must say that I am much more concerned about those of other than Canadian birth who have come here and been naturalized and are staying here and seeking to destroy our system, than I am with those who leave; in fact I think we should welcome the departure of many of those who come and do this.
It would seem to me that when an amendment is being considered which will widen the possibility of denying the rights of citizenship of those who leave Canada, or those who make declarations that amount to disloyalty to Canada or the abandonment of their citizenship, we should also consider the advisability of widening the basis upon which citizenship may be withdrawn.
I would of course wish that we were discussing this on a very much wider basis than it can be discussed upon the second reading of this bill. What I would prefer to be discussing at the present time is an amendment to the Criminal Code dealing effectively with communism in this country under a properly defined section of the code. In saying that I wish to make it perfectly clear that neither in my remarks now nor on any other occasion have I ever suggested that communism should be dealt with by name. That would not be effective. What I am suggesting is that the activities designed to undermine our democratic system in the service of a foreign power can be defined and should be defined in an amendment to the Criminal Code, which would apply to everyone, whether bom outside of Canada or within our


own boundaries. That, however, is not the subject now under consideration, and I therefore confine my remarks to possible amendments to the Canadian Citizenship Act, and the withdrawal of the citizenship which has been extended to those who have come to Canada and who leave here.
There are many people who have become naturalized Canadians who will not come within the amendments now before us. Let us take some of the examples. At the present time there are weekly publications in different parts of Canada which are published in languages other than English or French. They are generally described as foreign language newspapers. I am referring to those of the foreign language newspapers which are regular and vigorous advocates of communist doctrine. I might say that my remarks would apply with equal force to any publications which advocated what might be regarded as nazi, fascist or any other non-democratic doctrines. However, it is communism with which we are mainly concerned at the moment.
Men who have come to Canada and have been naturalized, and through that naturalization have gained the rights of free citizens of Canada, are week by week doing their utmost to undermine the confidence and the faith of newly-arrived citizens of this country by holding up to contempt and ridicule those institutions upon which we rely for the preservation of our freedom, and are making attacks on all those who are seeking to maintain the vigour and the strength of democracy itself. These people, given the rights of citizens, freely urge the support of those against whom young Canadians are fighting at this very hour. If that is not treachery, I do not know what can be described as treachery. Nevertheless it does not come within the legal definition of treason contained in the Criminal Code.
I am sure that in the Department of Justice there are those who are competent to draft an amendment to the Criminal Code which, without using the word "communism", or "fascism", or "nazism", or any other definitive doctrinaire word, will at the same time define with clarity disloyalty to Canada of that kind.
I believe that people who are doing that should be dealt with in the manner that is contemplated by the amendments now before us dealing with those who leave Canada to go back to their native land, or dealing with those who are convicted under laws now in force. To me it seems strangely inconsistent that we should be, on the one hand, awaiting a budget which call for the expenditure of $1,600 million for defence-defence against

only one possible enemy-and yet at the same time dealing with that enemy and his representatives in our midst with such gentleness and with such reluctance to recognize the danger for what it really is.
As I said before, I can only, within the terms of this act, deal with the citizenship of those who have come from other lands and become Canadians by naturalization. But the people who are trying to destroy democracy in Canada include within their ranks many of those who have obtained citizenship in that way.
Across this country there are communist organizations trying to undermine faith in Canadian democracy in many ways, not only through foreign language newspapers, but by means of the moving picture, by means of publications sold quite openly, and by other devices long employed for affecting people's minds and people's loyalty.
As the Department of Justice well knows, there are moving pictures in circulation in this country which have no other purpose than to spread propaganda in support of communism. In many instances that is being done by those who were born in other lands, have come to Canada and are now citizens of this country. There are also others within the same category who are running schools for young Canadians where disloyalty is the purpose of everything that is done. There again it should be possible to deal effectively with such people, just as effectively as with those who leave Canada to go back to the country to which these people are now expressing their loyalty.
I would urge the minister to give consideration to extending those definitions still farther. While it is true that there is not an amendment to the Criminal Code now before us, it is possible to introduce a definition of conduct of that kind within the Canadian Citizenship Act itself, which could be dealt with by the courts. If the Department of Justice is not prepared to put before this house an amendment to the Criminal Code, then I suggest that an amendment such as I have mentioned be introduced to the Canadian Citizenship Act; that a penalty be provided under which those guilty of conduct of that kind can be brought before the courts, and, if there is a conviction, citizenship should be lost in accordance with the procedure outlined in the amendments now before us.
I do not think the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) will question my statement when I repeat that I believe the officials of the Department of Justice do regard themselves as competent to draft such an amendment; because I am under the impression that he has such an amendment actually
Canadian Citizenship Act drafted, although he has not yet been prepared to put it before the house. I mention that only with the thought that it is most commendable that a condition of this kind should have led to the preparation of such an amendment. I hope that if an amendment to the Criminal Code is not made at this time, a further amendment to this act will be introduced when the bill is in committee.
In the event that anyone might suggest that others in the house should propose the amendment, my answer would be that if an amendment of this kind is to be effective it should be one put forward by the government. Administration is just as important as enactment; and if the administration of an amendment of that kind is to be effective, then such amendment must be in terms the government will carry out.
While I approve the amendments so far as they go, and will support them, I believe that the time has come for us to act in accordance with the scale and magnitude of the task we are undertaking, and that an emergency which calls for the type of legislation the government has already presented to the house for purposes of defence is one which should call for legislation that will deal more effectively with these traitors in our midst.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO REVOCATION OF CITIZENSHIP, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the speech from the throne it was announced that there were to be certain changes in the citizenship act. One or two of us perhaps had our own fears as to what those changes might be; but, having seen the legislation I can say now and at once that we are in agreement with what appears to be the purpose of the bill. After all it is only reasonable that when an individual renounces his citizenship he should officially lose it. It is only reasonable that when someone affirms allegiance to another country he should lose his citizenship rights in Canada. There can be no objection whatever to that.
However, there is a vital principle in the bill which I suggest requires some clarification from the minister, and should be discussed to some extent. We are told that an individual loses his citizenship when he is convicted in some court of competent jurisdiction of any offence involving disaffection or disloyalty to His Majesty. Those are fairly sweeping terms. I remember well that when the original citizenship act was before the house there was much discussion about a section similar to the one I have indicated. One of the things upon which members of all parties insisted at that time was that there should be equality of treatment for all Canadians, no matter in which
1574

Canadian Citizenship Act part of Canada they might live. It is conceivable that under this legislation there may not be that same equality. Appeal is to be permitted to ten different courts in the ten provinces. It is possible that the judges presiding over those courts will range from men of a most liberal turn of mind to those of the most reactionary. It is possible we may have ten different standards of disaffection; it is possible we may have ten different standards of disloyalty. In effect what we shall have will be ten different standards of Canadianism. That is something I would deplore, because it is the intention of all of us to try to secure equality of treatment for all.
There is another matter which has been discussed before, and which, some conceive to be an aspect of discrimination between those who are natural-born Canadians and those who have adopted Canada as their home. There are those who feel that the degree of punishment for the same offence should be precisely the same, and that the most serious punishment one could inflict upon anyone would be to take away his citizenship. That is the punishment meted out only to immigrant Canadians.
I am an immigrant, but I must say I view the situation in a somewhat different light. I came here of my own free will. I came to Canada because I wanted to. I knew what my rights of citizenship and my -obligations were going to be. I knew what my duties and privileges were going to be; and I was determined, so far as humanly possible, to live within the law of the land. I am convinced that from my point of view, and that of many others, no more serious hurt could befall one than to lose his citizenship. Nevertheless I believe that if an immigrant comes to this country and willingly and knowingly violates the law so that he is guilty of treason, he should lose that citizenship. There are others, among my colleagues, who were born in Canada, who would disagree with me.
The question arises as to exactly what disloyalty is. There are members of the house who advocated that Canada should be a republic. They would want to do away with the monarchy. They would abolish kings, and all the pomp and circumstance we associate with courts and kings. I disagree with them on that. However, I maintain they are entitled to their opinions, and if their opinions were to have the support of a majority I would accept the decision, as a good democratic citizen.
But is that being disloyal to His Majesty? Would one be disloyal if he were to advocate the setting up of a republic? Is there disaffection there, or is there disaffection when,


during the Easter recess, I go back to my constituents and raise the very devil about what the government is doing or is not doing? It is conceivable that under certain governments that might be regarded as sowing disaffection. On the other hand we must remember that during the thirties there were Canadian citizens who went back to nazi Germany and who, after serving a year or two in the German forces, came back to this country. In my opinion those men were traitors; yet the legislation was not adequate enough to cover them then. It is possible we have the same condition today among those who acknowledge allegiance to soviet Russia. In my opinion those people are also traitors in just as great measure.
What we want above all is to safeguard the citizen from the growing encroachment of government. I do not think that encroachment can be helped; it is one of those things which will happen. But it means we have to be doubly sure to see that the citizen is protected. It may be said: Well, after all, we have a minister who is a man of honesty and integrity, and upon whom we can depend. That may be so. I should be quite content to take the minister's word that he will carry out this legislation as honestly and faithfully as he can. But there is no guarantee that a minister of a similar calibre is going to follow him.
I recall the history of the 1919 strike in Winnipeg, when we had a somewhat different type of minister at Ottawa-and I am referring to Mr. Arthur Meighen. I remember well that on the occasion when ten Canadian citizens were arrested in Winnipeg and thrown into Stony Mountain prison, Mr. Meighen sent a wire to Winnipeg which read as follows:
Notwithstanding any doubt I have as to the technical legality of the arrest and detention at Stony Mountain, I feel that rapid deportation is the best course, now that the arrests have been made; and later we can consider ratification.
That was a most iniquitous thing to do. What guarantee is there that under some other minister it might not happen again? What protection is there for the citizen? That is what we are particularly interested in.
I remember during that same general strike in Winnipeg, when Mr. J. S. Woodsworth, the founder of this party, was thrown into prison for four or five days because he had the audacity to quote from the book of Isaiah in the streets of Winnipeg. That was then considered to be sedition. At times hysteria grows in any country until it becomes a serious menace. We hope that something like that will not happen again but we have to safeguard against it. Where the courts decide

that an individual has been guilty of disaffection or disloyalty the minister is to have the last word as to whether or not that citizen will lose his citizenship. As I said before, there is no more serious circumstance that could befall any Canadian.
The minister has the right to decide, and it is no reflection on the minister when I say that all of us who are elected members of parliament know what it is to be the victim of political pressures and political urges. While I am content to leave this right with the minister, I am not content to leave with him the right to have the last word. We suggest for the earnest consideration of the minister, partly as a safeguard for himself and partly as a safeguard for those who might be accused, that the individual should have a final right of appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada. That court is above all political pressures. That court is impartial. Let that court decide whether or not the individual should suffer the most grievous penalty of losing his citizenship. Were we to do that, then I think we would be restoring some of that equality for all which we desire. I hope that the minister will give this suggestion his most earnest consideration.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not usually take part in a debate of this kind, but to me these amendments are very simple. A man cannot be a citizen of two countries and be honourable and honest with both, just as the old book says that you cannot serve two masters. If a man is found to be using language, either in the press or vocally, that shows his disloyalty to Canada, he has no business to be a citizen of Canada. If he becomes a citizen of a foreign country, why should he want to be a citizen of Canada at the same time? I do not think we need to spend much time discussing these amendments, because they are so simple.
But I do know of one difficulty that is faced by a man who lives in the city of Fort William, which is considered to be made up of intelligent people. This man has raised a family but has not been able to obtain Canadian citizenship. I have always thought that after a person had been in Canada for twenty years, and had a good character, there would be nothing against his becoming a citizen; but this man has found that he cannot become a citizen of Canada unless he can answer all the questions.
I know a man who has lived thirty years in Canada and has reared a family that is a credit to Canada. They are all good athletes, good students and good university men, and yet the father is not able to be a citizen. I realize that these amendments do not cover 80709-1014

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to support the bill and to make a few remarks pertaining to it. So far as I can see, the chief purpose of the bill is to relieve a very few people of rights and privileges which by their own actions they indicate they do not value very highly. I say there are but a very few. I take this opportunity to reassure the great masses of new Canadians whose citizenship is cherished by possession that there is nothing in this bill that in any way prejudices their status.
As I say, the bill deals with two small groups of minorities. The first group consists of those who returned voluntarily to their native country to resettle and who endeavoured for their own purposes to retain some of the advantages they had gained by Canadian naturalization. What they want is dual citizenship; they want a privileged position. I cannot say that I have much sympathy for them. Dualism has been resolved in this country and we cannot tolerate it abroad. They cannot have it both ways.
No matter what inducements have been offered, no matter how rosy the picture was painted in order to get them to return to their country of origin, they automatically accepted life according to the dictates of the existing regime in that particular country, and the principal effects of such life, including a police state and forced labour, were well known to the most innocent of them. It scarcely seems reasonable for them to expect that their Canadian naturalization will exempt them from some of the unpleasantnesses that they found when they returned to the country of their origin. I imagine that they supplied more than their share of headaches to those countries as well as to ours, and this bill will reduce those headaches from six years to two years.
I said that there were two groups of people covered by this bill with whom I had. little sympathy. If I have little sympathy for the first group, I have none at all for the second. They are the people who sought and acquired the privileges and responsibilities of Canadian citizenship but who are really the servants of another state. In the course of that service they have betrayed the Canadian state. When their offence has been proved I can see no justification for their continued enjoyment of the citizenship which they have acquired, a citizenship which, by the way, not only gives them a fair trial and just sentence.
Because some of the persons involved in the recent espionage cases were foreign born,

Canadian Citizenship Act a regrettable shadow of suspicion has fallen inevitably on a large and intensely loyal section of the community. I say inevitably, because in all times of international stress there are suspicions that arise, and there is a flaming and a fading of tensions from time to time. I should like to repeat what I said on April 9, 1946, and I quote:
There have been those whose loyalty has wavered, who have imagined, in their confusion and in their woolly thinking, that there is a higher loyalty than that to Canada; who have not rated their acquired citizenship on so exalted a level as most of us have placed it. Recently we have been shocked to our very roots when we have had to face up to unpleasant realities which upset our comfortable and complacent thoughts and habits. There is no need to be alarmed. There is no point in hysteria, and there is no reason for losing our perspective. We have been tough with our enemies from without. We only need apply the rule of law in order to be tough with our enemies from within. That is what the law is for.
I went on to say:
Let me say a further word about loyalties. It is well that we look to the structure of our own nest before we inquire too deeply to see who has fouled it. Loyalty is a coin with two sides. On the obverse is the attachment of the citizen to the state; on the reverse are the service and inspiration which the state gives to the citizen. I have no use for traitors or for those who accept the protection and benefits of the state and then sell it down the river. I entertain no belief that loyalty can be divided, so much to the state and so much to another organism. To me, as to other members of this house, treachery in all its forms is despicable, and the oath of allegiance is not double talk.
About all I can do at the present time is broadcast the reassurance that disloyalty is the rarest kind of exception; that those who have won their citizenship through risk and labour tend to cherish it at least as highly as those to whom it has come as a birthright. But in the opinion of many the disloyalty of one reflects upon the integrity of the many. For this and other reasons I believe new Canadians as a whole should welcome this measure, which is designed to penalize and discourage betrayal. All those who have spoken already have indicated that they approach such legislation with one eye to the special dangers of the moment and the other upon the preservation of the traditional freedoms. One of those freedoms, of course, is the right to advocate social and economic changes; and most of us, no matter what our own views, will champion the right of the other man to express his. The house will note that paragraph (f) reads:
... if in Canada, has, by a court of competent jurisdiction, been convicted of any offence involving disaffection or disloyalty to His Majesty.
Hon. members will realize that a court will deal with this problem. To indicate that there is an awareness in high judicial places of what is going on in this country and in the world, I want to quote from a great judge

and a great Canadian, Mr. Justice Ivan C. Rand. Speaking in Toronto on March 30 he delivered the annual lecture sponsored by the Hillman foundation, established in 1946 by the amalgamated clothing workers of America in memory of the late president of the union, Sidney Hillman:
Mr. Justice Rand stressed the duty of judges to protect the nonconformist "against popular clamour, against any sort of subservience to that clamour or the betrayal from any quarter of our inheritance.
Our liberties are largely the accomplishments of such men. North America has been born of rebellion, rebellion in government, in church, in social organizations."
He went on to say:
The courts were constantly faced by the problem of determining the boundaries of individual freedom -the point at which individual action threatens the general security.
This could be determined by application of the rule of law, as opposed to the rule of man's despotism. It was insufficient to define freedoms without granting them to every citizen. The rule of law was the uncompromising rule of principle as against expediency.
He went on further:
Freedom of speech was also threatened by the discovery that it often was not exercised in good faith. Deceit had become an instrument in the propagation of an ideology, raising questions of the greatest difficulty in determining the point at which liberties must give way in order to maintain the wider security.
It is obvious to everyone in this house that the chief targets of this bill will be the communists. It is important, however, to make it very clear that the section is directed against them not because they are advocates of Marxism but because those it penalizes have become agents of a foreign state. It is one thing, for instance, for a man to attempt to convince his fellows that living conditions in the city of Omsk are better than those in Oshawa. That strikes me as a legitimate undertaking, though a bit foolish and I would presume rather thankless; but it is altogether different for a man to give his full devotion to another state and actively conspire against the country from which as a citizen he claims protection and all the benefits it may have in store for him.
Under this bill men will not be punished for their political beliefs but rather for their political treachery. I believe this bill is intended to make it very tough for traitors, which is as it should be.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I feel that I must say a few words on this bill. I cannot help feeling that it must have been with the greatest reluctance that a Liberal government felt it necessary to introduce a bill along these lines, just as it must be with the greatest reluctance that Liberal members will feel it necessary to

support it. I think one could safely change the word "Liberal" in that sentence to "Canadian" and it would still apply.
As the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) has so well pointed out, that we are faced with legislation of this kind at the present time is entirely due to the activities of those whom we lump together under the name of communists. The principle of this bill is not new, but the principle in the original bill is becoming broader all the time. Despite our hatred of communism and all it stands for; despite the danger which communism presents to us, we must not lose sight of other dangers that may be even more alarming. There is a great deal of talk throughout the country, and justifiably, about subversive activities. I rather wish we heard less of the word "subversive" and more of that very plain word "traitor" which was used a moment ago by the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll), because that word leaves no doubt whatever as to what is meant.
Because one sees dangers in the principles which underlie this necessary bill, that in no way means that one has the slightest sympathy for those subversive actors whom I prefer to call traitors; and I trust that we in this house may continue to separate the two sides, one the necessity of combating that sort of activity, and the other the necessity of protecting those things in our own mind which are our main justification for opposing totalitarianism in all its forms. I was bom and brought up in Canada in the days when we were British subjects and proud of it. I was brought up to regard the fact that I was a British subject as one of the most remarkable attributes which I could ever have; one of my privileges and one which imposed consequent duties.
In recent years the term "British subject" has become, for most of us, "Canadian citizen", and the same love of the term and respect for its implications I hope applies. There are those who have become Canadian citizens voluntarily. Perhaps they are entitled to more credit than I am. I did not become a Canadian citizen voluntarily but by an act of God. Those who have come to us from other shores have become Canadian citizens by their own choice. I assume the majority of them also place a value upon their Canadian citizenship, although most of us have taken occasion from time to time to regret that we did not emphasize that value sufficiently at the time we allowed them to acquire citizenship.
What I am leading up to, Mr. Speaker, is that I have, we all have, the greatest sympathy with the need and intent of this bill.
Canadian Citizenship Act There is not one of us who is not going to say "aye" when it comes to voting on the measure which is at least partially intended to protect this country against its enemies. But there is, sir-let us admit it-building up in this country a mass fear. Please note that I deliberately did not use the word "hysteria". I do not think there will be built up in Canada a mass hysteria, but a mass fear is being built up in this country. I am a victim of it. I believe that, to a greater or lesser extent, we all are. It is a fear to some extent of the unknown, which is a very dangerous fear because that type of fear is catching. It is, therefore, quite possible that we may fall into a trap and be carried too far. I do not want to lay myself open to a charge of international disrespect, but I suggest there are cases in the world today of mass hysteria from which we might take some lessons.
My purpose in speaking at this time in connection with a bill which takes away something from the individual is to urge upon the minister, the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), and the government of Canada that the greatest care be taken in the administration of this act. I know that hearings will be held in every case before a man can lose his citizenship. Mr. Speaker, what I hope not to see is dozens of hearings across the country because some well-intentioned individual thinks that someone else is not as loyal as he should be. None of us will object if we proceed expeditiously and relentlessly against those who are guilty, but heaven protect us from a wave of witch-hunting. We are not ready for it now, but I honestly fear that this wave of what I call mass fear might bring us to the position where we were almost ready to indulge in a witch-hunt, and that would be a great calamity in itself.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, and I believe that Canada believes in the principle that it is better for some guilty persons to escape than for one innocent person to suffer when he was not guilty. It is the innocent person, not the traitor, with whom I am concerned in connection with the broadening of these powers for taking away Canadian citizenship once lawfully acquired. I would say to the government, and through them to those who will administer this act as well as to those who may be considering amendments to the act: Do not make it too easy to deprive a man of his citizenship, because for once I agree with the member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Stewart): there is nothing that we can give of greater value than Canadian citizenship.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO REVOCATION OF CITIZENSHIP, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the beginning I should like to associate myself with the remarks of the

Canadian Citizenship Act hon. member who has just taken his seat (Mr. Applewhaite) and to say that, like him, I hope and believe that we shall not give way to hysteria or witch-hunting, the evils of which he has not exaggerated in the least. I should like also to associate myself with what was said by the member for Spadina (Mr. Croll), and to join with him in saying that I hope what we call new Canadians will not regard this as in any way derogatory to their status. I would even go beyond what the member for Spadina said. I believe that we will find in many new Canadians a prizing of their citizenship perhaps far beyond the value which those of us who have always been Canadians attach to it. I have met many new Canadians who have made me feel that if there was the same devotion to this country on the part of a large number of the old citizens, it might be a much better place.
It was only today that I carefully read this paragraph in the speech from the throne, and I observed the use of this wording:
Appropriate amendments to the Canadian Citizenship Act will be introduced to prevent the retention of Canadian citizenship . . .
It is only today that I realize the use of the word "retention" is intended to indicate that it applies to those who have received it and, therefore, not to natural-born Canadians. It is with regard to that general question that I should like to make a few comments along the lines taken by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew), as to whether notwithstanding our approval of this bill we might not like to see something wider dealing with the situation.
I observe that when we debated this question a year ago I quoted a remark made by the minister of external affairs which he had made during the summer of 1949. At page 2130 of Hansard for May 3, 1950, I find the following:
He . . .
That is the minister of external affairs.
. . . told the Montreal Rotary club the domestic threat of communism must be met . . .
Here are his words.
. . . "by strengthening, if necessary, our Criminal Code, against actions which threaten the security of the state.
I quote that and I remind you, Mr. Speaker, there was a reference to the Criminal Code made this afternoon by the leader of the opposition. I wish to stress what we have stressed before, that we are not advocating a witch-hunt. We are not advocating any attempt to penalize people for what, in Japan, they called dangerous thoughts. The only thing we are talking about is overt acts. The point we question is whether the code is adequate. Having regard to the fact that
[Mr. Macdonnell (Greenwood) .1
nothing has been done since the minister of external affairs made that remark, I think it would be relevant to ask the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Harris) to tell us this afternoon whether, in fact, the government has decided that nothing along that line needs to be done.
There is another thing that is a good deal in my mind, and it came out in the debate a year ago. I do not think communism would be nearly so dangerous if it only appealed to evil people, people whom we ordinarily characterize as undesirable. The thing that bothers me about it-I attempted to bring this up a year ago-is that it has a strange appeal to people whom, from many points of view, we must concede to be high-minded, good people, however completely misled they seem to be. I quoted at that time briefly, and I will quote again, from a book called "The God that Failed", and which brought out what I think is a fact and what I think accentuates our danger. I quote briefly from page 6 of the introduction which was written by the well-known English leader Crossman. Speaking of the intellectuals-and there were six intellectuals who contributed to this book -he asked this question:
How could these intellectuals accept the dogmatism of Stalinism? The answer is to be found scattered through the pages which follow. For the intellectual, material comforts are relatively unimportant; what he cares about is spiritual freedom.
And again Crossman says:
-the communist novice . . . wearied and worried by the privilege of freedom-getting relief by subjecting himself to the canon law of the Kremlin.
I read that quotation to the house partly because it called up to my mind an incident that happened to me a short time ago when I was visited by one of what I suppose you would call the followers of Mr. Endicott. He and a couple of other people appeared at my room one day and I had a short talk with them, and remonstrated with them for what seemed to me to be the extraordinary folly of their attitude. I might have been occupying my time more profitably, I expect. When they raised the question whether we were justified in holding the views we do hold about Russian despotism, I said: "What do you make of the case of Czechoslovakia?" One of these young men said to me: "Would you be surprised to know that I was at a demonstration in Prague last summer? We were all together, students, police and others, and we were celebrating in honour of peace. What would you think about that?" I said: "I would think it was one of the finest bits of arranged propaganda that I had ever heard of in my life." There you are, Mr. Speaker. There were young men, perhaps more or less sincere, who had been completely taken in by that propaganda.

I have another thing here that I want to read to the house because it indicates the kind of thing that is going on and which to me makes it much more serious than it would be, as I said a few minutes ago, if it was the kind of thing that appealed only to the hard-boiled people of the type that we always regard as undesirable, who are selfish and who are ready to break the law for their own ends. I hold in my hand a publication called The Frontier. It is a new publication. I do not know much about it. I think it is a respectable publication. I think so partly perhaps because the issue previous to the one I hold in my hand argued that we should have regard to the common-sense laws of economics when we were thinking about the various social measures that we should pass. That seemed to me to be a sensible remark. Perhaps I am therefore predisposed to regard this as a sensible publication. It is called The Frontier, "a Christian commentary on the common life". Here is the monthly letter, February, 1951. It has some things to say about communism and its appeal which I present to the house because I have to confess that I was extremely slow to believe that communism had in it the danger that it has. I was slow to believe that the kind of people one meets and finds agreeable, and with whom we share many common thoughts, could have a department of their life in which they were able to do things which to me were almost incredible. I read briefly from this publication:
Current Christian literature about communism, including some that comes from missionary societies and notably from China, has a good deal to say about its revivalist power. Converts to communism, especially the young, embrace it with a zeal and ardour, for the works as well as the faith, that often greatly impress Christian observers. They see college students, boys and girls at school, and unlettered workers responding to the appeal of what they believe is a message of world salvation and undergoing a new, severe discipline with complete self-abandonment.
Then I skip a few lines and continue:
But it is also important to get this fact of communist fervour in perspective and not to be romantic about it: for it remains true that what is propagated as a messianic faith marks the bid of a minority for political domination, and only a minority within that minority consists of sacrificial zealots and idealists. George Orwell wrote-and he had some first-hand knowledge of the matter-that a revolutionary is oftener than not a social climber with a bomb in his pocket.
I have thought it worth while to mention this because it seems to me that those of us who find it difficult to believe the kind of things that go on should remind ourselves occasionally of such facts as what I have just read. I always remember a German refugee, who had become a Canadian citizen and who had a profound loathing of the
Canadian Citizenship Act nazis, saying to me in June, 1940, just when the war really broke out: "Regard nothing as fantastic". By that he meant we could expect almost anything to be done. He was thinking particularly of sabotage. Incidentally, I have always thought that we owe a great deal to the police during those subsequent years for the fact that so little was done. But I mention that because I think it comes back to the point that I raised at the outset: whether in fact there is a broader situation here that we have not wholly dealt with. A phrase was used this afternoon, I think by the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll), referring to these people as agents of a foreign state. I confess that to me it is often unreal- something I have to pinch myself to remind myself of-that no doubt one is meeting every day and, for all one knows, perhaps eating at the same table with-I am not referring to the House of Commons-people who might be described in that phrase. I therefore say to the minister, it seems to me that what is being done is sound, although there may be points of detail that should be amended. But I put to him this broader question, and it is really the same question put by my leader: Is he satisfied and is the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson), whose words I quoted although they are now more than a year old, satisfied that nothing further needs to be done beyond this rather minor and limited action which is now being taken?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would not rise and speak in this debate unless I thought I had something to contribute to it. In that respect I fancy that I am the same as those who have already spoken on this bill. Much has been said this afternoon in respect of certain phases of citizenship rights which prove perhaps to be disloyal to His Majesty the King. It has always occurred to me that the time to nip disloyalty in the bud is before the bud begins to bloom. In that respect I therefore think that we have reason to be particularly careful as to the type of people or, shall I say, the attitudes of the people to whom we grant citizenship. I am quite cognizant of the fact that the government has safeguarded this matter to some considerable extent in its present legislation. I have, however, one suggestion to make in respect of that particular matter. I know of course that a person coming to this country from some other country cannot just suddenly pick up and become a citizen. There are certain rules, regulations and procedures to follow, and he should not be given his citizenship until it is pretty well proven to the authorities that he is worthy to become a citizen. My suggestion, however,

Canadian Citizenship Act is that there should be a number of citizens who sponsor the application of one desiring to become a citizen. I would go slightly further. I would suggest even that the application be given some notice in the press. I would go so far as to say that the names of those who are sponsoring the application should appear in the notice. I would go one step further and say that those names, together with the applicant's name, should appear not only in the official publication, which is the Canada Gazette, but in some more widely circulated periodical, preferably the daily press in the particular community in which the person lives.
The reason I am making these suggestions is that I do not think one who may be accused of disloyalty or disaffection is perhaps entirely to blame. A man is in a sad state of affairs when he has no friends. I am of the opinion that his friends, and particularly those who would have to sponsor his application for citizenship, must bear at least part of the responsibility of what might turn out to be disloyalty or disaffection.
I am passing that suggestion on to the minister. I notice that during the debate he is taking notes, and I should like to have him express his views in respect of the suggestion.
As I see the bill there are just one or two further comments that I would care to make. One is respecting the fact that when disaffection has been proved the person loses his citizenship. I should like to dwell on that for just a moment. To me, and to the most of us, citizenship as Canadians is a very precious thing. On the other hand I should like to venture this rather modified observation. What advantages are there in citizenship? That may be a rather striking observation, but let us examine it carefully. A person comes to this country. He enjoys the courtesy of Canada by being able to stay in this country; and just so long as he behaves himself he is permitted to stay. He can invest his money; he can go into business. Under certain conditions he can seek employment, and he can enjoy all the rights of citizenship except perhaps the right of the franchise and the right to hold public office.
Looking at it in that way I am wondering whether the loss of citizenship is such a great penalty to impose upon one who is disloyal to the country. Just what would it matter to him anyway? Therefore I am inclined to agree with the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) that some more drastic steps should be taken to deal with those who are disloyal, or, in the words of the bill, are convicted of an offence involving disaffection


to His Majesty, or which might be interpreted as disloyalty to our particular way of life. I recall as an illustration of what I am talking about carrying on an election campaign.
Some of us have been through a number of elections. I recall that in this particular campaign I had one man who was a particular opponent of the position which our party took. I am not saying that he was an opposition candidate. I do not want to leave that impression. No, he acted purely within what I would suppose to be his rights, namely, the right of any citizen to be able to express himself as our right of free speech gives him. But he followed me to some of my meetings. He tried to cause trouble. He was a vigorous opponent of what I was trying to proclaim. And after the campaign got well under way, in fact it was almost terminated, I began to wonder whether or not the chap was going to decrease my expected majority. I began to get a little bit disturbed. Someone came to me and said: "Oh, Hansell, you do not need to be afraid of him. Why, don't you know that man is not even a Canadian citizen." I was rather surprised at that. I do not mean to imply now that he came from some-oh, well I will put it this way. The gentleman was an American. He was farming in our part of the country and had farmed there for a good many years. It was taken for granted that he was a Canadian.
I found that he was not a citizen and never intended to become a citizen; yet here he was taking all the advantages of citizenship, even to entering into the position of influencing public opinion in an election campaign.

Well, he was taking part to

I go a step further and say that what will make citizens really proud of their citizenship is to make effective in Canada our

particular way of life, so that the citizens of Canada can enjoy the freedom we profess, and enjoy it with that standard of prosperity and quality of living that this country, with its vast wealth and with our free democratic concept, is able to give its citizens.
Before taking my seat I wish to make only two further observations, and I make them on the basis of what was said a short time ago by the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Stewart). He delivered what I considered a most excellent speech, one with which I agree almost one hundred per cent. I cannot say I agree the full one hundred per cent because, of course, he does not belong to my party. For that reason I shall have to depreciate my agreement with him to the extent of a fraction of one per cent at least.
However, he did bring out a point in connection with the interpretation of disaffection. I fear that there is a weakness in the measure in that respect. After all, under this measure a minister of the crown will have the final decision. I do not suppose this government would be guilty of what I am about to suggest, and I am quite certain the minister would not, but the interpretation of the section could be broad enough to hold a club over the head of any citizen who might oppose vigorously some principle or policy His Majesty's advisers might be pursuing.
I recall the early days of the movement this group represents. During the days from 1930 to 1935, when we were proposing monetary reform and were exposing the iniquities of this burdensome debt-creating monetary system, some of our opponents were so bitter that they declared publicly some of us should be locked up because we were proposing things that would upset entirely our whole economic system.
Some may smile. I see the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) smiles, and I hope he does so because he believes such a proposal to be ridiculous. I thought he was going to answer and say that he did think it was ridiculous; however, he remains silent. Therefore I shall say for him that it is ridiculous.
We can say what we like about communism and about those people who are now at the head of the peace movement but I am convinced that some of them are conscientious in their approach to the problem. They lean over backwards in their pacifism, and they have been imbued with the ideas they now pursue. Whether it be they or whether it be other persons who are opposed to the status quo, such people are going to be looked
Canadian Citizenship Act upon with some suspicion. Who knows but that the interpretation of this section involving disaffection might not be so wide that it would affect the free expression of our people. I think the minister might give some consideration to that point-and no doubt he has, because he would not be presenting the bill if he had not.
I shall conclude by supporting the suggestion of the hon. member for Winnipeg North that there should be some final court of appeal, even to the extent of appealing a decision by the minister. Such a course would remove the matter completely from the political arena, and would leave it with our courts, so that justice could be rendered on the merits of any particular case. I support the hon. member in his suggestion, and I hope the minister will express himself in regard to it.

Mr. Speaker, it was stated by an hon. member opposite that it would have been difficult for the Liberal party to ask this house to enact this kind of legislation. As far as I am concerned, had I been a member of the cabinet, I should not have hesitated to ask the house to enact it, chiefly because I -am a staunch believer in Liberal principles. I would have been pleased to suggest to this house that the facilities which are given people from abroad to enter this country and to enjoy the rights of Canadian citizenship are too great and ought to be curtailed, for in certain cases, one may question those people's intentions.
I think this is an excellent bill, and I have no objection to conferring upon the hon. the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Harris), or the governor in council, the prerogative or authority to decide to whom this amendment to the Canadian Citizenship Act shall apply.
Those who in this house or elsewhere advocate a distinctly Canadian flag and national anthem are often considered as faddists. But such is not the case. In fact, those symbols have a very deep meaning for the Canadian citizen, and especially for the person who wishes to become a Canadian citizen. They help him understand how proud he must be of the privilege of Canadian citizenship. It is our duty to show these new Canadians the value of the privilege of being a citizen of a country like Canada and there is no better way of showing that than by having a national flag and a national anthem. Such symbols would make them prouder of being citizens of this great Canada because, even if our population is not large,

Canadian Citizenship Act we belong to a country whose unlimited resources can make it one of the greatest in the world. Besides, in the matter of exports our country ranks third and we can surely improve our position in other fields if all our citizens, by birth or naturalization, understand the value of this North American country.
I fail to see how this legislation could interfere with certain freedoms. I have always felt that freedom should not be granted equally to good and to evil. To those who enjoy Canadian citizenship, who believe in one philosophy or other, whether it be historic liberalism, Marxian socialism or what is called Fabian socialism, I say that a doctrine which is bad overseas is equally bad in Canada. To those who ask for the privileges of Canadian citizenship and who use these same privileges in an effort to destroy our public men and undermine our institutions, I say they have no right to those privileges.
We all seek to enhance the prestige attached to Canadian citizenship. We must therefore prevent anyone from outplaying Canadian authorities in certain fields, philosophy, in particular.
I congratulate the government for introducing this bill in the house. It certainly is justified. I feel we should thank our leaders because those who have long been unafraid to raise their voice against Marxist communist ideologies now see their warnings seriously heeded. I would even like the bill to be more drastic. In my opinion, those who leave this country under the pretext of returning to the paradise in which they were born should be compelled, before they are allowed to come back to this country, to go through a certain period of probation so as to prove that their mind is now free from the ideologies which first drew them back to the land of their birth, and that they will not again engage in activities detrimental to Canadian citizenship.
I would like the bill to go further. I may seem radical, but I believe that evil should not be permitted to operate freely and equally with good. A doctrine that is bad overseas is equally bad in Canada.
I am sure that the public will accept this amendment to the Canadian Citizenship Act. I dare say that a large proportion of our people who understand how right we are in asking that restrictions be applied to certain individuals will rejoice in the fact that the
[Mr. Gauthier (Portneuf) .1

government is taking all necessary means to ensure that Canada is never faced with what many, even today, consider to be only an imaginary threat but which is a real danger, since the enemy is on the prowl, waiting for the proper moment to pitch into us, if I may be permitted that common expression. I hope the public will realize that our fear is not imaginary, for we see only too clearly the methods and the means used by Marxist communist propaganda to preach that doctrine in our country, almost openly.
