Mr. Speaker, one of the reproaches of democracy in our country as well as in many others is that so little value is placed upon the privilege of citizenship. It may be because we make citizenship so easy to obtain. It may be that in the case of those who are born in this country something may still be lacking in the inculcation in minor years of an appreciation of the duties as well as of the privileges of citizenship. It may be that, in the case of those who acquire citizenship in Canada through the machinery of the citizenship act, we have not been as careful as we should have been with respect to the preparation of such persons, both for admission to Canada and then in turn for admission to the privilege of Canadian citizenship.
I have been pleased with one note that has run through this debate, as it ran through the debate on the introduction of the citizenship act in the 1946 session, that we in this parliament are now beginning to reflect the desire and purpose that throughout Canada a higher value shall be placed upon the possession of Canadian citizenship. It seems to me that if we achieve that end we shall have contributed not a little to the strengthening of the basic bulwarks of democracy in Canada.
There is one other note that has been sounded in this debate this afternoon which, it seems to me, was timely and proper. I refer to the concern that citizenship shall not be taken away arbitrarily from those who now possess it. There are so many dangers in interfering with freedom of expression that this parliament, as the champion of the freedoms of Canadians, must be most alert and vigilant that nothing be permitted, if

we can prevent it, by the way of infringement upon the right of free expression which is one of the great embellishments and privileges of Canadian citizenship.
I am sure that the house received with pleasure the reassurance of the minister when introducing the bill this afternoon as to the intent of the department in administering the provisions of the act. There may be something lacking in section 19 of the act, and properly reference has been made to this fact this afternoon by several hon. members who have spoken. It is true that under section 19 of the act no citizen may be deprived of his citizenship without a hearing before a commission, if he desires an inquiry by a commission. We have in section 19 the clear provision that such a commission shall be presided over by a person appointed by the governor in council who holds or has held judicial office. That is a salutary provision, and undoubtedly is a most valuable safeguard in connection with the exercise of the powers under section 19 of the act. Of course, it will apply also to the amendments under consideration today. However, there are one or two features of that right which I think the house might well consider. For instance, attached to that right to a hearing before a commission is the proviso that, if the governor in council thinks fit, instead of being held by a commission any such inquiry may be held by the superior court of the province in which the person concerned resides.
That immediately raises the question whether it might be better to have these inquiries held by the courts. The suggestion was made this afternoon that in any event, even after one of these inquiries by a commission, it should be open to the person concerned to carry an appeal to the courts. It would be interesting to learn in connection with the inquiries held to date under section 19 (4) of the Immigration Act, how many have been held by appointed commissions and how many by the superior courts of the provinces. No doubt the minister has some statistics on the point, and I hope that at some stage of the debate he will give the house that information. It seems to me that with language like this in the act there could be no objection on the part of the government to providing either that all inquiries shall be held by superior courts or that there should be the right of appeal to the courts before an executive order is made by the minister depriving any individual of his precious citizenship.
As to the amendments themselves, Mr. Speaker, I am bound to say that the bill
Canadian Citizenship Act before us is of much more meagre proportions and much narrower effect than I for one had expected. I re-examined the appropriate paragraph in the speech from the throne to which the minister made reference this afternoon in moving second reading, and found these words:
Appropriate amendments to the Canadian Citizenship Act will be introduced to prevent the retention of Canadian citizenship by persons who have renounced their allegiance or shown by their conduct that they are not loyal to Canada.
Unquestionably many members of this house placed an interpretation upon that paragraph which is not borne out by the bill now before us; either that, or there has been some change of purpose on the part of the government in the intervening two months. Certainly the impression that went abroad was that the amendments the government proposed to introduce would be more rigorous and far-reaching than those we find in the bill. As a matter of fact the scope of this bill is quite narrow. It will be observed in the first place that it amends only one section of the citizenship act, namely section 19. It applies, of course, only to naturalized, and not Canadian-born citizens. Even within those narrowing confines the bill purports to confer the power of cancellation of citizenship upon the minister in only two cases, broadly speaking. The first case is that of the citizen who has taken up residence abroad under circumstances which indicate that he is transferring his domicile back to the land from which he first came. The second is the case of the individual who has been convicted of an offence involving disaffection or disloyalty to His Majesty.
May I just dwell on that latter provision for a moment. I should think the house would require, either from the minister or from the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson), some elucidation of those words "offence involving disaffection or disloyalty to His Majesty", particularly in comparison with the language of the present act, which is different. In the present act the conviction which is a ground for the deprivation of citizenship on the order of the minister is conviction of treason or sedition by a court of competent jurisdiction. At first blush one would say the words "offence involving disaffection or disloyalty to His Majesty" would cover more ground than treason or sedition, but I think the house will wish some clarification of the words in this amendment. What offences are involved there apart from those already covered by the present act, treason or sedition, and the other that comes to mind, namely, an offence under the Official Secrets Act? I think the house will desire that information from the minister.

Canadian Citizenship Act
There is one observation of a detailed nature I think might properly be made in connection with these provisions. What is to follow when the minister has made an order cancelling the citizenship of any individual who has offended the provisions of section 19? One immediately asks, does it involve deportation? Well, under the present citizenship act, of course, no question of deportation is involved. In all fairness, I suppose under the amendments one would say that where the individual has resided outside Canada for two years in circumstances which suggest that he does not intend to return, no possible question of deportation arises. Even there, however, it might be a nice question if that individual returned and sought to enter Canada. He could not enter as a Canadian citizen, but he might contend that he was a resident of Canada. There is nothing here touching his status under the Immigration Act, it seems to me. It might be well worth the time of this house to consider what further incidents should attach in a case of that kind, where in a clear case an order has been made taking away the citizenship of an individual who has left the country.
But let us take the other case, in which the individual has been deprived of his citizenship because of conviction of an offence involving disaffection or disloyalty to His Majesty. Suppose it is not a conviction of the serious offence of sedition or the even more serious offence of treason, but on a charge under the Official Secrets Act. What happens after he has been convicted and sentenced, and served his term? There are provisions in other legislation in regard to deportation, but it seems to me this house ought to include within the ambit of its consideration of a measure of this kind the question of what is to follow in such a case.
I refer to section 41 of the Immigration Act to see what light it may throw on this question of the right of a citizen who has been deprived of his citizenship under this act by order of the minister because of having committed one of the offences which are grounds for deprivation, to see what may be the position of such a person under this section of the Immigration Act. Section 41 has remained in its present form, without amendment, since 1928. It took that form in that year by amendment of the previous section which goes back to 1919. The language of this section, it seems to me, offers an interesting comparison with the language of the amendment now before the house. It reads:
Whenever any person other than a Canadian citizen advocates in Canada the overthrow by force or violence of the government of Great Britain or Canada, or other British dominion, colony, possession or dependency, or the overthrow by force or

violence of constituted law and authority, or the assassination of any official of the government of Great Britain or Canada or other British dominion, colony, possession or dependency, or of any foreign government, or shall by word' or act create or attempt to create riot or public disorder in Canada, or shall by common repute belong to or be suspected of belonging to any secret society or organization which extorts money from, or in any way attempts to control, any resident of Canada by force or threat of bodily harm, or by blackmail; such person for the purposes of this act shall be considered and classed as an undesirable immigrant.
Then follows a provision dealing with the machinery attaching to his being classified as an undesirable immigrant and the right of deportation provided by the act.
One naturally asks how this language, in the view of the Department of Justice, compares in breadth with the language of the amendment; in other words, where the offence involved is disaffection or disloyalty to His Majesty. Does it follow from the terms of section 41 of the Immigration Act that every citizen who is deprived of citizenship because of the conviction of an offence involving disaffection or disloyalty to His Majesty, immediately becomes subject to deportation, or is it the view of the Department of Justice that the language of section 41 of the Immigration Act is not as broad in some respects as the language of the new clause to which I have just referred? I think, Mr. Speaker, particularly having regard to the note sounded by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) in his speech today, that this question of what follows, so far as the individual is concerned, the order of the minister depriving him of his citizenship is one of high importance. If the effect of the order is simply to deprive a man of his citizenship and leave him free to exercise all the other privileges enjoyed by persons in this country, it may be that we shall have fallen short of taking the steps that ought to be taken in the light of an offence so serious as that involved in disaffection or disloyalty to His Majesty, particularly in dangerous times like those in which we are living.
The minister may say that is not a matter for the citizenship act. That may be, Mr. Speaker, but it certainly is a matter that ought to be considered when we are addressing ourselves to an amendment of this kind. I well recall that in 1946, when the bill embodying the citizenship act was under debate in this house, the relationship of many of the provisions of the bill to those in the Immigration Act received very careful consideration in the house. It was the subject of a protracted debate.
One wonders, for instance, in considering this provision, about such cases as the one we have been reading about in the newspapers lately, the case of Freda Linton, now

I believe Mrs. Freda Linton Alexander. If after her residence in the United States she is now being returned to Canada, a question will naturally arise. If she was born in Canada-I do not know whether she was- it is obvious the provision in this bill could have no application to her. If, on the other hand, she was born outside of Canada and acquired citizenship in Canada, and is now to be brought to Canada before this present legislation comes into effect after more than two years in the United States, is this legislation going to have any application to her? lit would be interesting to know whether her return, under some compulsion from United States authorities, would have the effect of depriving the minister of any jurisdiction under the language of subsection (d) which applies to residence abroad of not less than two years. If Mrs. Alexander is returned to Canada in this way, what is to be the effect of this section in such a case? As I say, I do not know whether Freda Linton was born in Canada, but I think that her imminent return, as we read about it in the newspapers, may raise some interesting questions as to the effect of subsection (d).
I observe also, Mr. Speaker, that we are not informed by the government as to what, if anything, is to be done in the case of those persons who are travelling abroad under Canadian passports which have been procured by false pretences or under improper representations. You will recall, Mr. Speaker, that that subject was the basis of one of the important recommendations of the royal commission on espionage in 1946. We have heard very little about any attempt on the part of the government to give effect to that important recommendation. It seems to me that the use of a Canadian passport obtained by a person who, born abroad, has obtained citizenship in Canada and obtained a passport by false pretences, should be carefully considered, as to whether that ought not also to be made a ground for the revocation of citizenship. We know that there have been abuses of passports granted by the proper Canadian authorities.
I share with those who have expressed themselves this afternoon a concern that no citizen of this country should be arbitrarily deprived of his citizenship by executive action or decree. It would be a situation fraught with the greatest danger for Canadian citizens if it were open to any minister, by irresponsible or ill-advised action, to deprive a Canadian citizen of this very high privilege and possession, Canadian citizenship, apart from a clear offence against the provisions of the act.
Canadian Citizenship Act
It may be, Mr. Speaker, that the enactment of legislation of this kind will have a salutary effect, not simply in giving power to the minister to enforce a rigorous measure against persons who commit offences against the act, but also in dissuading persons from committing such offences. It may be that this measure will exert a little more restraint upon those who do not value adequately the high possession of Canadian citizenship, and do not show His Majesty that loyalty which is properly required of every Canadian citizen, and everyone who enjoys the protection and benefits of living under the laws of Canada.
One may be pardoned in conclusion for expressing, as others have done in this debate, amazement that there are still some people in Canada who are prepared to place a lower value upon Canadian citizenship, freedom under Canadian institutions and Canadian laws, a part in the precious Canadian heritage, than the subscription to a foreign doctrine that is based upon a denial of God, a denial of the right of the individual to freedom, and the right to worship God in his own manner according to his lights.
It simply Alls one with amazement that people who have lived in Canada, and Who have acquired this great privilege of Canadian citizenship, should still be prepared to place that citizenship in jeopardy by preferring to follow a foreign ideology whose political direction with all its revolutionary purposes is directed from the Kremlin today, an ideology which	demands-as	we well
remember from the evidence taken before the royal commission on espionage in 1946- a higher loyalty than the individual or citizen owes to his own country, regardless of what that country may be or his rights and privileges in it. Yet that is the political essence of this foul doctrine which some people in Canada, even after living here, even after acquiring Canadian citizenship, are still prepared to value more highly than their rights in this country.
Where cases are proven of offences of that kind, Mr. Speaker, there should be no delay in applying the law according to its full rigour. There should be no hesitation in enacting rigorous laws in this parliament and in calling for rigorous enforcement of those laws, as long as we safeguard the rights of the individual by permitting him to go to the courts, in order to assure him that there will be no arbitrary application of the laws or arbitrary decision under the laws simply because parliament gives to the minister a right to revoke citizenship in the case of an individual. There, it seems to me, is the proper course that ought to guide parliament in a case of this kind. Let us maintain the

Canadian Citizenship Act right of the individual to go to the courts in order that there may be no arbitrary exercise of executive power, but in defining the offences which give rise to the power to take away from people rights of which they have proven themselves utterly unworthy, I for one would not hesitate for a moment in asking parliament to proceed to enact rigorous laws and in calling upon the government for the rigorous enforcement of the laws so enacted by parliament. It seems to me that while this bill goes a little distance in that direction, it is not one that really carries us very far toward coping with the broader problem with regard to those who are showing themselves daily to have much more love for and loyalty to this foreign ideology directed by the government of another country than they have for freedom and for Canadian institutions. I hope that some time the government, as the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) called upon them to do, will give the house an opportunity of dealing with legislation in proper form-with proper safeguards of the rights of the individual, with proper protection of his right to go to the courts-dealing with this question of disaffection and disloyalty that we are seeing expressed in many forms in many places in Canada today.

speechtext: Before passing from section 1, I think it would be appropriate that the minister should indicate whether there is in fact any thought in the minds of the government that they will proceed under any other legislation to deal with communists or similar activity in this country. I think it is appropriate that this information should be before the members of the committee because, whether rightly or wrongly, at the time of the speech from the throne there was a good deal of comment in the press which placed a wider interpretation upon the reference in the speech from the throne to this legislation than the bill now before us justifies. In many newspapers across Canada there was the suggestion that the government at last were going to come face to face with this issue and that they were going to pass from the stage of twilight peace to some measure of reality in facing what they regard as an emergency in other cases but as not so much of an emergency apparently in this. For that reason I think that, before we pass from this section which calls for general remarks, we should know whether the government at this session intends to introduce any other legislation pertaining to communist activity in this country.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO REVOCATION OF CITIZENSHIP, ETC.
speechtext: As the leader of the opposition has indicated, the press comment at the time the speech from the throne was delivered speculated on what the particular reference to the citizenship act might mean. Nevertheless, it must be obvious, and it is obvious from what he has just said, that to be effective and to do what he recommends, any amendment to the laws of this country would be made by the Minister of Justice through the Criminal Code or through some other form of statute. The citizenship act is confined to the granting and the revoking of citizenship; and in my opinion it should not be the vehicle of any other form of legislation to apply to a particular group of people. Under those .conditions, Mr. Chairman, I suggest that our consideration this afternoon is related to the present amendment to the citizenship act. If the government should at any time decide to take the action that the leader of the opposition suggests should be taken, I am quite sure that notice of it would be given on the order paper in the normal manner, and would reach the house in that manner.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO REVOCATION OF CITIZENSHIP, ETC.
speechtext:
I do not think that the remarks made by the minister in any way meet the situation. The act we have under consideration, and particularly the amendments included in this act, become a vehicle for bringing under the effect of this act other legislation such as the legislation to which I have referred and which I have suggested should be adopted. The section before us for consideration would provide that where an offence had been committed under the Official Secrets Act or under the Naturalization Act, and the courts had found anyone guilty of an offence under those acts, then under this act the governor in council could deny continuing citizenship to those who had been guilty of that offence. It is for that very reason that I have suggested that we should know at this time whether it is intended to introduce an amendment to the Criminal Code which will deal with those activities related to communism or any similar foreign invasion of our rights by the methods that are best known to us in relation to the communist party in this country at the present time. If something is not to be done to deal with those activities, then this act is substantially inadequate to deal with the major activities of communists, either of Canadian birth or of foreign birth, who are seeking to destroy our democratic processes at this time.
If, on the other hand, there were to be another act dealing with this subject, then this provision would be very much more effective, and could have much wider consequences. It was with that thought in mind

that I asked the question; and I did observe that the minister very correctly pointed out that the introduction of an amendment to the Criminal Code would be done by the Minister of Justice. I think it would be proper, if the government has reached a decision, that the Minister of Justice should indicate to us now whether any amending legislation along that line will be introduced. I would point out before I sit down, in the hope that the Minister of Justice can indicate that something of that kind is to be done, that it was not only the press which drew conclusions which went beyond the apparent intention of the government. There was before this house a bill introduced by a private member, which would deal with certain aspects of communist activity. It will be recalled that when that bill was called on the order paper the hon. member who had placed the bill before the house stated that he did not propose to proceed with it at that time because of his expectation that the government did intend to deal with this matter as indicated in the speech from the throne.
I need not do more than point out that the hon. member who was putting forward this legislation perhaps had better opportunity than I have to know the views of the government in regard to some matters which are discussed elsewhere than in this house. For that reason I think it would be appropriate that we should know before we pass from this first section of the bill whether the Minister of Justice has any thought of introducing legislation along that line.

The words are my hon. friend's. I do not think that I would even necessarily agree with his meaning.
It is a matter of the most elementary knowledge of any member of any legislative assembly that government policy originates sometimes in the minds of the ministers and sometimes in the minds of ranking civil servants and others who pass the suggestions on; and that in the course of considering changes of policy it may be necessary, in order to crystallize views upon it, to secure a draft of these ideas in the form of an amendment to an act; and then that draft is considered. I am not suggesting that this practice is being followed in respect to the draft amendment to which I referred a moment or so ago. Such a draft may be considered first of all by a committee of civil servants, and then get to a committee of the cabinet, and finally to the cabinet itself. It is not until it has been considered by the cabinet, and until the cabinet has reached an opinion upon it and it is brought into the house as a matter of government policy, that it is something for which the government is responsible.
Wishing to be as helpful as I can to my hon. friend I really do not think that the government in this case, or in any other case, is called upon to say at the present stage what decision it will reach with respect to Criminal Code amendments which have not yet come before the government for consideration, but which are in the course of preparation and will come before it in due course.
As soon as that decision is reached I shall be very happy to introduce the Criminal Code amendments bill in the ordinary course. At that time my hon. friend will have the opportunity of debating the provisions of that bill. If the bill does not contain the provisions which he desires, then he will have the opportunity of reproaching us for not having included them when we come to consider the estimates of the Department of Justice. I am afraid that beyond that I cannot help my hon. friend very much.

speechtext:
I have a number of comments to make on the debate as soon as I can get the opportunity. Dealing with the one point raised by my hon. friend and followed by the hon. member for Eglinton, there is in section 19 an alternative manner of revoking citizenship. The process begins with a notice to the citizen that it is the intention of the minister to revoke his citizenship for stated reasons. Upon the receipt of that the citizen can then request a hearing before the revocation commission. Under certain circumstances the governor in council may, instead of having that hearing before the commission, have it before a judge of a superior court. I am informed that that procedure has not been taken in the past, but that all the hearings have been before the commission.
When the commission hears the evidence, including that of the citizen, they make a recommendation to the minister, who then may or may not revoke the citizenship. I also want to assure the committee that in no case has the citizenship been revoked when the commission recommends that it should not be revoked. In other words, the minister has accepted the recommendation of the commission not to revoke citizenship in every case. I may go further and say that there are cases in which the citizenship is not revoked despite the recommendation of the commission.
If my hon. friend thinks that when this commission makes its recommendation the minister should then make a decision and that thereafter there should be an appeal to a judge of a superior court, I suggest that it is a new thought, and one which was not brought before the house during the debates of 1946.
I think it must be obvious that the very existence of the commission, comprised, as it is, of a judge, and several citizens, indicates that they would protect the citizen, quite as much as would a normal judicial proceeding in court. For that matter I think there are many citizens who would prefer to have it done in that way, rather than with the publicity which would attend a court. Nevertheless we can give consideration to the suggestion. I do suggest however that this body is quite as impartial as one would obtain in any other proceeding, and I doubt if a further appeal is necessary to protect the citizen.

speechtext: Then, Mr. Chairman, as I requested during my remarks on second reading, may I ask for some elaboration of the expression in paragraph (f) "any offence involving disaffection or disloyalty to His Majesty" as compared with the language of the present act, and the expression, "convicted of treason or sedition." Is there anything more involved in the expression, "any offence involving disaffection or disloyalty", than in the expression "treason or sedition", apart from offences under the Official Secrets Act? If so, what are those additional offences?

speechtext: Perhaps this is a matter which should be passed upon by the Minister of Justice. The fact is however that we have in mind the Official Secrets Act. We are not aware of any other act at the moment which would come within the meaning. There may however be acts of espionage which would not come within the Official Secrets Act-although I think it is fairly broad. But the expression "disaffection or disloyalty" is known to all acts dealing with citizenship, and the revocation of it. It is taken directly from the United Kingdom act, and is employed there. As the hon. member knows, it was employed recently in revoking the citizenship of Dr. Fuchs. That kind of disloyalty and disaffection is what we have in mind.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this bill is for the revocation of citizenship, in certain cases. It does not affect civil rights at all, because an alien has the same civil rights as has a

full-fledged Canadian citizen or British subject. As it does not deprive anyone of civil rights, I wonder if it would not be more simple to check the list in the hands of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police setting out well-known communists, and then pass an order in council to deprive them of their public rights, and to deprive them of their Canadian citizenship-because they are not worthy of enjoying it.
In these times we hear a great deal about fundamental freedoms and human rights, for scoundrels. Honest men have been accused unjustly, men who could not defend themselves successfully before the courts. Yet we hear long tirades from Mrs. Roosevelt about scoundrels, the scum of the earth, who come here and, in the name of British justice, ask to enjoy fundamental freedoms and human rights. Yet they are the ones who advocate the denial of human rights and freedoms to others.
Why should we be so lenient with those people? It would do them no harm, it would not give them a toothache if they were deprived of Canadian citizenship. They should never be allowed to enjoy or exercise it. That is simple; it is not complicated.

Would the
hon. member explain what he means when he refers to being deprived of public rights?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO REVOCATION OF CITIZENSHIP, ETC.
speechtext: To be deprived of public rights is to be deprived of citizenship. My hon. friend, who is a learned jurist, knows very well that public rights go with citizenship. Aliens cannot exercise them. If my hon. friend were an alien he could not run for parliament. A public right given to a communist means that he can run for membership in the House of Commons, that he can vote at municipal elections, that he can run for office in a city council, a provincial legislature or anything else. He could even be appointed to the bench.

Well, that is logical. I do not see why we should be so considerate of those people who try to undermine the pillars of our Canadian society. "Human rights and fundamental freedoms"-I am sick and tired of hearing that all the time in the house, because it is for the benefit of communists who have no other purpose than the broadening of legislation for their own benefit.
When the Department of Citizenship and Immigration is so hard on Count de Bernon-ville, I do not see why Tim Buck is not expelled from Canada and deprived of his citizenship. This I cannot understand. And there are others in Montreal, including Guy
Canadian Citizenship Act Caron, who are enjoying full Canadian citizenship, although they are well-known communists.
Surely there is something wrong there. Then, there is something in the bill that does not suit me. The suggested wording of section 19(2) is as follows:
The governor in council may, in his discretion, order that any person shall cease to be a Canadian citizen if, upon a report from the minister, he is satisfied that such person has, when not under a disability,
(a)	when in Canada and at any time after the first day of January, nineteen hundred1 and forty-seven, acquired the nationality or citizenship of a foreign country by any voluntary and formal act other than marriage:
(b)	taken or made an oath, affirmation or other declaration of allegiance to a foreign country; or
(c)	made a declaration renouncing his Canadian citizenship.
According to what has been written about communism, as we see it in books and periodicals, a communist is a man who has no allegiance to His Majesty the King, or to the chief of state or to anyone who is not a communist and a vassal of Moscow. It is easy to understand that. Therefore it is not on the report of the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration that the government should act, but on the report of the Minister of Justice to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration, giving him the list of names of avowed communists in the files of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. Is that fair enough? That is my suggestion. I do not intend to move an amendment, but I do suggest that if there is injustice to anyone he should be given the right of appeal to the minister or notified, as the minister said a moment ago, of what proceedings are about to be taken.
I challenge any communist to deny that he is a supporter of Stalin. I challenge him to deny Stalin in public. Whether he is under oath or not means nothing because they do not believe in an oath even though their heads are covered. I hope that some action of this kind will be taken, if not now at least tomorrow. Hundreds of communists are enjoying special privileges in this country. The government knows what communism is and it has no sympathy for them. Why should these people be treated like newborn babes who are wrapped in cotton and bathed in olive oil? No one should be afraid to act with regard to communism and to stop it it at the earliest possible moment.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO REVOCATION OF CITIZENSHIP, ETC.
speechtext:
This afternoon the hon. member for Skeena enunciated what I thought was an admirable doctrine. He said that he would rather see two or three guilty individuals go free than one

Canadian Citizenship Act innocent person punished. I revert again to this subject. The minister has outlined for us the steps which can be taken by an individual to protect himself. I am not so much concerned about what will happen while the present minister is minister because I think his conduct is exemplary. He has been generous in his treatment of many cases. But I am concerned about what some other minister may do. That is why I want to see all the protection possible given to the individual, even though he may be guilty. I want to see him get all the protection to which he is legally entitled, and much more so if perchance he should be innocent.
That is why I suggest that the individual should have the right of appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada and not to the higher court of a province. The stripping away of citizenship is a most serious thing indeed. Would it not be fairer and perhaps wiser to give the individual the alternative of stating whether he wants to be heard by a commission or by a superior court?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO REVOCATION OF CITIZENSHIP, ETC.
speechtext:
To begin with, almost all countries follow the commission practice. It is a more informal procedure and does not burden the courts with cases which in many instances would remain on the list for two or three years before being heard. I think I can show my hon. friend that it does do justice to the citizen concerned. While I have not been in the house all the time, I do not think that any complaint has been made in the house since 1947 about any case handled by a commission.
One can argue that the judiciary is the best body to decide all questions of this kind. That may well be, but I think the committee will agree that if we removed that decision to the courts there would be members of this house who would feel that we had made a mistake. They might argue that the place to debate citizenship, how it can be gained and how it can be lost, is here, and that the minister should be responsible to the members of this house and through them to the people of Canada as to whether citizenship should be revoked. That is why we retain the present system. I think it is a good system and unless my hon. friend can point to errors in it I think we should continue with it.

subtopic: HUTTERIAN BRETHREN CHURCH

speechtext:
The house in committee on Bill No. 7, to incorporate the Hutterian Brethren Church- Mr. Viau-Mr. Dion in the chair.
On section 1-Incorporation.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
subtopic: HUTTERIAN BRETHREN CHURCH
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, on the various occasions this bill has been called I have asked that it stand. I am obliged to the hon. member for St. Boniface for his courtesy in permitting that to be done. This bill was introduced in the Senate, where it was referred to the private committee and finally passed. In this house it has also been con-

sidered by the private bills committee, where it was thoroughly looked into. As far as I know no question has been raised with respect to it in either committee. Having asked that the bill stand on previous occasions, however, I thought I should give some explanation.
The people who are seeking the incorporation of this religious order are a particular sect who live for the most part in Manitoba and Alberta. In Manitoba they are located mainly between Winnipeg and Portage la Prairie; and to be even more precise, for the most part they live in the municipalities of Cartier and Portage la Prairie.
These people follow a strict, communal type of life, entirely different to anything else we have experienced in this country, and they follow that type of life religiously and conscientiously. Perhaps they can be best likened to a hive of bees, except in the matter of their thrift. They live in colonies, with a common dining room and common living quarters. Theirs is a common income, with no one being paid individually. But the time comes when each colony, which may number fifty families or more, finds it necessary to expand, and they swarm out wherever they can secure new property. In this area to which I have referred I believe there are something like twenty of these Hutterite colonies, located in the very best farming district in the province, and naturally when they expand they remain as close as possible to the existing colonies. Only last week I had the privilege of seeing a map of that area showing the Hutterite colonies, and it was somewhat alarming to say the least to see how they have expanded there. I am bound to say that if this goes on, in the course of time they might very easily acquire all the property in that district.
The point I am making is that while these colonies now have in the neighbourhood of
70,000	acres, their expansion would mean the acquisition of more property, which would make it almost impossible for those following a different sort of life to remain in those communities. Collectively the Hutterites are a large organization, and are good financial risks. As a result they are able to purchase large tracts of land, and in so doing they completely upset the community life. They dislocate the schools and other community enterprises. More than that, the neighbours do not find it congenial, to say the least, to reside close by. The result is that sooner or later these people acquire the properties of their neighbours as well.
My reason for asking that this bill stand on the various occasions it has been called
Hutterian Brethren Church is largely due to a very deep concern that has been expressed by the non-Hutterites of all classes in the community where these people have become established. Some two years ago these non-Hutterites formed themselves into a loose type of organization and made representations to the provincial legislature, requesting that steps be taken to bring about a larger measure of control, though I do not like to use that word. They asked that something be done to assist in bringing about a better relationship between the people who follow our way of life and the Hutterites. Certain things were done, but fundamentally little progress was made. I mention this in order to indicate that there is a very real concern in that area of Manitoba regarding these people. And we are not alone in that concern. I believe our friends in Alberta had a similar experience, and took certain steps to meet this very situation. One of the things Alberta did was to require that no new colony should be established closer than forty miles from an existing colony. I am bound to say I have a large measure of sympathy with that proposition. These people have shown no indication of any desire to be pioneers. As I said a moment ago they have resources, and being a collective corporation they are able to obtain credit and purchase land as a private individual cannot do. In other words, they are a good credit risk for anyone who wants to sell them property or do business with them.
I say that the Alberta government, in my view at least, took a rather reasonable course. I do not think it hurt the Hutterites at all, because I think it was to their advantage since it gave them an opportunity to see what they could do in other lands that were neither so fertile nor so well established as those on which they were residing. As an indication that I am not alone in raising some apprehension over this particular matter, I refer to a speech made in this chamber one or two years ago by the member for Calgary West, who was much more critical than anyone else I have heard in connection with these people.
The fact is that these people have no desire to become assimilated in this country. They follow their own religious beliefs. They do not want to educate their families, and they just do not want to pioneer or do anything except to live their own lives in their own easy way. We may say that is a perfectly sensible course to pursue. However, I do not believe any of us would feel that our country was developing or making much progress if everyone in it were a Hutterite. I have never known the children of the

Hutterian Brethren Church Hutterite colony to go to high school. I have never known one to enter any profession, that is they never become lawyers, doctors or anything of that kind. It may be their way of life, but I am bound to say that to me at least it does not give much confidence for the building of citizenship among those people.
I refer again to what I indicated a moment ago, that they have no desire to become assimilated with other people. Now that is what causes the apprehension among those people who are residents of the same community. They would regret exceedingly to see these people, who have not assumed the full rights of citizenship-incidentally they do not vote except in municipal elections to a limited extent- secure any advantage at this stage. As I said a moment ago, they do not appear to be prepared to assume the full rights of citizenship as we understand such rights in this country. It is for that reason that my friends, largely in my own constituency have expressed so much concern over a course of action taken by this body to acquire federal incorporation. I have done my best to satisfy them that this bill does not provide any encroachment by these people; that it is no different, in the main, from legislation that is provided for other religious organizations.
I confess that I am not a lawyer, nor am I an expert at reading legislation that is presented to us. We have however taken advantage of the opportunity of getting free legal advice. This bill has been reviewed by some of my lawyer friends, without cost to anyone. I think I am able to say to the member for St. Boniface that this bill is in conformity with similar legislation that has been introduced in this house for the incorporation of other church organizations, and on that score alone I have no intention of delaying the passage of the bill. But I do want to take this opportunity of reciting a few things in connection with these people to indicate why there is this measure of concern about them, and why we should exercise a measure of caution when dealing with a class of people who are not prepared to become assimilated in the way of life that we recognize in this country.
So far as the bill itself is concerned, any comparison I have been able to make of it with similar legislation that has been introduced into the house concerning other church organizations does not reveal that it is out of line at all. Just in passing I would say these people have a perfect right to introduce what is contained in section 6. These people have always been conscientious objectors. I understand that they have felt some concern over that principle of their religion because

they fear others might attempt to cloak themselves under the mantle of the Hutterite Brethren church. For that reason, as I understand it, the main purpose of this bill is to get definitely established who can become a member of the Hutterite church. I think we will subscribe to that immediately, and hope it will work out to their advantage as well as to the advantage of the rest of the people of Canada.
In looking over the bill some of my friends did express a good deal of apprehension with respect to section 7 which has to do with the power to acquire and hold property. I might say that the fear in this regard was that federal incorporation might mean these people could combine their collective resources, and thus become a great monopoly to acquire properties and other things of that character without limit. I am assured that that is taken care of under our provincial laws having to do with property and civil rights, so I do not think we need to have any apprehension in that regard. I only mention that for the sake of the Minister of National Revenue and the Minister of Finance, and to urge them to look over matters of this character to see that it is not a means of cloaking an organization of this kind under the guise of a religious organization, thereby avoiding income tax.
The only other matter to which I wish to refer is what I assume to be the governing clause. It is contained in section 10 which says:
. . . the exercise of the said powers shall in any province of Canada be subject to the laws of such province as to the acquisition and holding of lands by religious corporations, in so far as such laws apply to the corporation.
I take that to be the governing factor in connection with this bill, and if it is I am quite satisfied to have it go through as it is. Perhaps I should mention one other thing. The member for St. Boniface paid high tribute to these people in introducing the bill, as did the hon. senator who introduced it in the other place. I am obliged to them for that, and I do not quarrel with the observations that they made. I believe I can say I have been a little closer to this problem than either of those gentlemen. I do not say that in a critical sense at all, but I should like to suggest to them that, in spite of the good qualities they have attributed to these people, there are many little irritations, not of great importance in themselves, which from time to time arise. It is perhaps because of their method of living which irritates our own people in those particular districts. I refer again to their method of doing business. They purchase largely on a wholesale basis, and strange to say they can usually get ample

credit to do so. Everything tnat they can, they make themselves. They make their clothing, their boots and shoes.
Consequently you can understand how there is a good deal of displeasure with regard to these people in the local communities that are affected. I think that one of the mistakes that we made in our own province was with respect to the question of education. These people do not believe in educating their children. Our mistake was that we did not require them to attend our public schools as other children did. They have, for the most part, lived within our school laws; but being a community, being really little towns in themselves, it has been convenient to locate the schools on their properties. Consequently, there has not been the opportunity for the children of these people to get out and take advantage of outside education; and I think they are the losers by it.
One could say other things regarding these people. I rose only for the purpose of voicing a serious feeling on the part of the people in the communities that are affected. They are apprehensive over the growth and the expansion of these colonies. They realize and recognize immediately that it is upsetting the ordinary community life as we have recognized it in our development from the first time this country was opened up. While I am not one of those who say that these people have not the right to follow whatever religious faith they choose to follow, none the less I think that there should be a greater recognition perhaps on the part of our own province of the particular problem that has arisen because of these people. I said a moment ago that I had a good deal of faith in or support for the action taken by the province of Alberta in requiring that these people should not create a new colony any nearer than forty miles from an existing colony. I said that I thought that was to the advantage of the Hutterites themselves, and I believe time will bear that statement out. If these people would go out farther afield and become more or less pioneers, I would think they would be appreciated more than they are.
But in connection with the efforts that were made by this same committee to which I referred in the province of Manitoba, immediately any suggestion was made that there should be a curtailment of freedom or any thought of an attempt at restricting their religious faith, naturally the hue and cry went up throughout the country that we were interfering with human rights and fundamental freedoms or whatever you may call it in that regard. Even the press of Manitoba took that line and pressed it
Hutterian Brethren Church severely. I want to say to the press of our own province that if they had to depend on the Hutterite people for their circulation, they would soon find that it did not amount to very much; because I will venture to say that there are not a dozen daily newspapers from the city of Winnipeg sold in all the Hutterite colonies in the province of Manitoba. Likewise there are no radios or musical instruments-nothing that we look upon as cultural necessities in our way of life.
Perhaps I have said enough at this stage. I am obliged to the hon. member for St. Boniface for not pressing consideration of this bill until those who were particularly interested-and I think that is democracy- had an opportunity to have it carefully reviewed and to be assured that there was no undue advantage being taken by federal incorporation of this group of people at this time.

Section agreed to.
Sections 2 to 6 inclusive agreed to.
On section 7-Power to acquire and hold property.

The house resumed, from Friday, March 16, consideration of the motion of Mr. Applewhaite for the second reading of Bill No. 116, respecting British Columbia Telephone Company.

Mr. Speaker, this bill is described as an act respecting British Columbia Telephone Company. It provides for amendments to the act which set up that company quite a few years ago. The main amendments will be, in the first place, to increase the capital from $25 million to $75 million; in the second place, to make certain changes in the provisions covering preference shares; and finally, to give the company the power to pay a commission on the sale of its shares.
I am opposing the bill in its present form for several reasons. I believe that the people of British Columbia are not getting a fair deal in so far as telephone rates are concerned; that the telephone users in our province are not adequately protected now, and that their position will be worse if the bill passes in its present form. Parliament has a responsibility to protect the people of British Columbia, and I ask for the most careful consideration of the bill by my fellow members.
It is significant that the Vancouver city council passed a resolution unanimously, asking the members from that city to oppose this measure on two grounds:	In the first
place, because the council believe that an excessive increase in capital is being sought, and second, they believe that under the company's present act there is no protection against unreasonable charges which are levied against the British Columbia Telephone Company by its parent and affiliated companies. In other words, the Vancouver city council believe that the British Columbia Telephone Company is being milked by its parent company in Montreal, and by the parent company of the Montreal company, which is an American corporation, with headquarters in Kansas City. All the time the
British Columbia Telephone Company people cf British Columbia have to feed the cow by way of paying the full rates.
I use the words "the people of British Columbia" not the words "the people of Vancouver" advisedly, because this company and its affiliates own over 90 per cent of the telephones used in that province, and of course they have a monopoly in all of those areas. I believe that all of the communities in our province endorse the stand taken on this bill by the council of the city of Vancouver. Last year there was a hearing before the board of transport commissioners of an application by the company for an increase in telephone rates. At that hearing the city of Vancouver was represented by counsel; also the cities of Victoria and New Westminster, the municipality of Burnaby and the Union of British Columbia Municipalities, and the provincial government. All of these bodies appeared opposing the application of the telephone company for an increase in rates.
The city council now ask that the increase of capital be kept to a reasonable amount. This bill seeks an increase from $25 million to $75 million, which means that the capital would be trebled. But that is not the whole picture. In 1947, just four years ago, the company obtained an amendment in the House of Commons which increased the capital from $11 million to $25 million. So that if the increase now sought becomes law it will mean that within four years there has been almost a sevenfold increase, from $11 million to $75 million.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that in this bill the company is asking too much. At the rate hearing last year it said that it had large expenditures to make on capital account. There is no doubt that there will have to be a great deal of money spent in the years that lie ahead. I understand the evidence was that it would require about $10 million a year, by way of new capital expenditures, until the year 1952 which would mean a period of three years, and that there would be further expenditures in later years. The sponsor of the bill, upon introducing it in the house, said the company would require $10 million a year for ten years. I rather think that was an exaggeration. The annual reports for the years 1949 and 1950 show that the company has spent something like $8 million in each of those years. I would point out to hon. members that because of shortages of materials there will probably be a good deal of difficulty in these years lying ahead to get the necessary supplies. I doubt very much whether it will be necessary or, in fact, possible, to spend as much as $10 million a year.

British Columbia Telephone Company
However, let us look at the picture showing the money to be spent on capital account. In the treasury now there remains $5 million. In other words only $20 million of the $25 million has been issued. If this increase of $50 million is granted there will then be $55 million available to issue as shares. But the ratio of share capital to the bonded indebtedness in financing by this company is approximately 40 to 60. In other words where they raised $40 through the issue of shares, they raise $60 by issuing bonds and other securities of a similar nature. So that if they have $55 million in share capital available to issue, they would have $82,500,000 to be raised by way of bonded indebtedness. This makes a total of $137,500,000 which would be available for capital expenditures, if the bill is accepted in its present form.
Even at their own figure of spending $10
million a year, the increase they are now asking would be good for from fourteen to twenty years. I would point out that in addition there is approximately $17 million in a depreciation reserve, which would also be available for capital expenditures. I say that fourteen to twenty years is too long a time for the company to go, without being required to come back to parliament.
And it is so important that parliament should have some check on companies of this kind. There is no check by the provincial government. The company is incorporated under a dominion act, and is not subject to regulation by the provincial utilities body. The only groups which have any power of regulation are right here in parliament, and also in the board of transport commissioners. So I say there is great value to the people of British Columbia in the requirement that the company must come before parliament at fairly frequent intervals.
Always the situation is that the people pay the shot. In the long run, any increased expenditures have to be paid by the telephone users; and those users are entitled to all the protection they can be given by parliament. The present bill asks for too much at one time. It means that there will be much less control by parliament-in fact there will be no control for from fourteen to twenty years. It means there will be no control by the cities and municipalities of British Columbia. And those corporate bodies are always at a great disadvantage in trying to fight a utility company such as the British Columbia Telephone Company.
I know very well that there is need for a pretty close check on the company, because when in 1947 they applied for the increase from $11 million to $25 million I thought I

had worked out a pretty good method of making sure that there would not be an application for an increase in rates in the immediate future. When the bill was before the house for second reading I asked for an undertaking from the then hon. member for New Westminster, who was sponsoring the bill. Hansard of that time, where the undertaking is recorded, reports my words as follows:
I understand that the hon member has been authorized to give assurance to the effect that the company has no present intention of applying for an increase of rates and will not make any such application unless compelled to do so by extensive changes in conditions.
Mr. Reid answered, "That is my definite understanding". In so stating he was acting in perfectly good faith for he had been authorized by the company to give that undertaking. Then I went on to say:
That assurance is clearly worded and contains a statement to the effect that an application will not be made unless the company is compelled to do so and then only by reason of extensive changes in conditions. If the hon. member for New Westminster is prepared to give that assurance on behalf of the British Columbia Telephone Company I for one shall have no objection to the bill passing.

I am authorized to do so, and it is my
definite understanding.
That was in May of 1947. In June of 1949 the company launched its application for' an increase in rates. The Prime

The legal position of an alien leaving Canada is governed by the Immigration Act which provides that an alien acquires Canadian domicile "only by having his domicile for at least five years in Canada after having been landed therein." He loses his domicile by "voluntarily residing out of Canada with the present intention of making his permanent home out of Canada and not for a mere special or temporary purpose."
Thus a Yugoslav citizen, regardless of the length of time he has lived in Canada, will lose his right to re-enter Canada if he goes to Yugoslavia with the intention of making his permanent home in Yugoslavia. Should he change his mind and wish to re-enter Canada, he would have no right to reenter Canada and would have to apply for admission as any other prospective immigrant.
Moreover, if he should be readmitted to Canada, he could not count his previous stay in Canada for the acquisition of Canadian domicile. In order to become a citizen of Canada he would, after his return, have to remain in Canada for five years.
The legal position of a Canadian citizen by naturalization leaving Canada is governed by sections 20 and 21 of the Canadian Citizenship Act. Section 20 reads in part as follows: "A Canadian citizen, other than a natural-born Canadian citizen . . . ceases to be a Canadian citizen if he resides outside Canada for a period of at least six consecutive years," subject to various provisos. Section 21 provides inter alia for cancellation of citizenship by order in council if a naturalized citizen "out of Canada has shown himself by act or speech to be disaffected or disloyal to His Majesty."
It is important to note that a warning appears at the back of the current Canadian passport, which reads as follows:
"Canadian citizens by naturalization certificate or citizenship certificate should bear in mind that unless under the laws of the state to which they originally belonged or by the provision of a treaty, they have ceased to be subjects of that state, their certificates have no effect within its boundaries nor can the good offices of His Majesty's representatives be extended to them there."
There is quite a bit more to the statement, but I am not going to read more of it. I am going to use this as the basis of a question which I hope the minister will answer during this debate. It happens that the exception in sections 41 and 42 is an exception in favour of a Canadian citizen, so that those sections do not apply to a person who is a Canadian citizen.
My understanding of the sections is this, that if a person is convicted of an offence involving disloyalty and disaffection, and thereby loses his citizenship, he does not at the same time suffer the further penalty of deportation, because the act having been performed while he was a citizen he is exempted under section 41. However, if he subsequently commits any of the acts mentioned in sections 41 and 42 he then becomes subject to deportation, because he is not at that time a Canadian citizen.
Nevertheless it ought to be clear that when a person is accepted as a Canadian citizen after residing here five or more years deportation does not follow too easily upon an offence under sections 41 and 42. The other country of which he was a national or a citizen before becoming a Canadian citizen might possibly object to the subsequent deportation. That is a matter which has to be arranged on every occasion.

speechtext:
Before we leave this section, may I say that the discussion has been helpful in clearing up a number of points in connection with the Canadian Citizenship Act, and the purpose of the amendments before the committee.
I am sorry the Minister of Justice is engaged elsewhere because, before leaving this subject, I would have wished to point out to him that I was quite aware of the general amendments to the Criminal Code, but that this particular amendment is something of a special nature-that is, the amendment which was under consideration.
The adequacy or otherwise of the amendments now before us will very largely be determined by whether or not there is other legislation which does make it possible to deal effectively with communists in this country who are actively seeking to undermine our system. Commendable though the intent and purpose of these amendments may be, this is a very limited attempt indeed to deal with an extremely important subject at a time when we are told the very survival of our nation and of our civilization is at stake.
The minister has explained that 219 citizenships were revoked last year, of which some were already out of Canada. This is but a small fraction of the number of the people who are actively engaged in this country today in subversive activities not now satisfactorily covered by any existing law. I am not only concerned with the possibility of dealing with those born outside of Canada and outside the British commonwealth; I am concerned about the possibility of dealing effectively with citizens who were born in this country. In fact I think the citizen who was born in this country, and whose traditions were anchored here long before the others came, is a worse offender than the man who comes here and perhaps must learn something of our traditions.
I do however wish to follow the remarks made this afternoon by the hon. member for Spadina, when he placed some emphasis upon the loyalty of the overwhelming majority of those who have come here from other countries. It would be the desire of every member in the house to understand that nothing said here would create any impression that members of the House of Commons, in any party, have in their minds the thought that there is any lack of loyalty on the part of those who have actually made the decision to become citizens of this country. In fact, the very choice they have made in many cases creates a more conscious sense of vigorous loyalty than may perhaps exist in the minds of those who accept as a matter

Canadian Citizenship Act of course the privileges they possess as citizens of this country. Nowhere will one find more vigorous expressions of loyalty to Canada and our great institutions than in the gatherings of those people who are truly loyal to Canada, to our democratic institutions, and to the ideals we are seeking to advance in our daily lives. They, I believe, are the very ones who would welcome most warmly some evidence that it is going to be possible to deal effectively with those who are seeking to implant in Canada a kind of life that they know only too well, from their own associations, and which they know in a way we do not quite understand. Those people who have lost fathers and mothers, brothers and sisters or wives under this vile form of despotism are the ones who know best how far we should be prepared to go in preventing any of that type of activity being carried on here in Canada.
Before we pass on from this discussion of citizenship, may I once again emphasize my belief that it is very important that we have a law which will define this offence, not only so that offenders may be dealt with, but so that there may be evidence of that very concern which has been expressed, that no man shall be deprived of his rights as a citizen, except under the law.
That is happening today. The government of this country has stated, with some display of satisfaction, that it has removed from employment those suspected of communist activities. If people are going to be deprived of the right to earn their livelihood, and to be deprived of that right by the most important employer in the country, then I say that first of all there should be an offence that can be defined. I say we are actually inviting that very disregard of the right to employment and citizenship that we are saying we should preserve, when the government of the country, as the main employer, says, "We are dismissing these people because they are communists; but we cannot define 'communist activity' or activities of the nature that should be dealt with in this way."
I think it would be agreed that there have been few people more vigorous than I have been in condemning communism. But I certainly believe the government of this country should be the first to see that, if people are going to be deprived of the most basic of all rights, namely the right to work, and if they are to be deprived of the privilege of maintaining themselves and their families by their work, there shall be a real offence defined by law.
rMr. Drew.]
We want to establish the rule of law, and the government should be the first to insist upon it. So, in passing from these remarks on citizenship, at which time I had hoped we might have had some assurance that there would be an amendment to the Criminal Code to deal with this subject in a wider field, I once again seek to impress upon the government my belief that if there is something which in the view of the government should deny to a man the right to employment, then the government should decide to instruct the officers of the crown to define that very offence with which they are dealing.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR ELECTED REPRESENTATION IN TERRITORIAL GOVERNMENT AND APPOINTMENT OF JUDICIAL OFFICERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the principal purpose of the bill is to give the population of the Northwest Territories elected representation in the territorial government by providing for the election of three members in a council of eight. The other five members will be aopointed. The details are set out in the bill and explanatory notes. I should like, however, to say something about the recent developments in the Northwest Territories which have led the government to propose the changes embodied in the bill.

Northwest Territories Act
When the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta were created out of the Northwest Territories in 1905, the remaining portion of the territories, although large in area, contained a very small population and was of limited economic importance. The Northwest Territories Act, 1905, therefore provided that the territories should be administered by a commissioner acting under the instructions of the governor in council or the minister of the interior, and that a council of not more than four persons might be appointed by the governor in council to assist the commissioner in the administration of the territories. Until 1921, however, no council was appointed, and during these sixteen years the commissioner of the Northwest Mounted Police acted as commissioner of the territories.
In 1921, consequent upon the increasing public interest in the territories arising out of the discovery of oil, the act was amended to provide for a council of not more than six. In the same year the deputy minister of the department of the interior was appointed commissioner of the territories, and six councillors were appointed, all being senior officials of federal departments having an interest in the territories. The system thus inaugurated in 1921 has continued to the present time, the sole change being that since 1947 a resident of the Mackenzie district of the territories, who is not a government official, has been appointed a member of the council. This change was a first step towards giving the residents of the territories representation on the council.
Generally speaking, the original population of the territories was Indian and Eskimo, the Indians being largely confined to that portion of the Mackenzie district lying south of the tree line, and the Eskimo population to the Arctic coast of the Mackenzie district and to the Keewatin and Franklin districts. In 1941 the population of the territories was 12,028 divided among the three districts by races as follows:

The estimated population of the territories at the end of 1949, compiled

In recognition of the substantial increase in the permanent white population of the Mackenzie district, the residents of that portion of the Mackenzie district lying east of the 109th meridian of west longitude were given representation in this house in the last redistribution of seats.
The government considers that the time has now arrived when provision should be made for elected representation in the territorial council. A fully elected council and its logical corollary, an administration located within the territories, seems to be a proper objective at which to aim. I do not feel, however, that it would be wise to achieve it in one step. To begin with, the territories are still greatly dependent upon the financial support of the federal government. Thus, in the fiscal year 1947-48 some $7,758,865.20 was spent in the territories from federal funds, while the revenue accruing to all federal departments from the territories was only $640,323.44 or about 8 per cent. Similarly in the fiscal year 1948-49 some $9,778,646.20 was spent in the territories from federal funds, while the revenue accruing to all federal departments from the territories was $719,517.98; and in the fiscal year 1949-50 some $7,963,388.72 was spent in the territories from federal funds, while the revenue accruing to all federal departments from the territories was $720,073.90 or about 9 per cent. I should think the people of Canada generally would expect the people of the territories to be capable of bearing a larger share of total government expenses in the territories before they can reasonably expect to have a fully elective council.
The present proposal, by conferring upon the population of the territories the opportunity to elect three members of the territorial council, will, I hope, be a step toward ultimate fully elected government. The length of this transitional period will depend upon factors affecting the rate of development of the population and resources.
There are several other minor amendments in the bill, which are fully dealt with in the explanatory notes. I will only mention one of these. It is proposed to add to section 34 of the Northwest Territories Act

a subsection giving to the governor in council power to appoint officers for the due administration of justice. At the present time section 10, subsection 1, paragraph (1) of the act gives to the commissioner in council authority to define the powers, duties and obligations of sheriffs; but paragraph (j) of the same subsection specifically excludes from the powers of the commissioner in council authority to appoint such judicial officers. The volume of judicial business in the territories now makes it necessary to appoint sheriffs. The proposed amendment provides the necessary authority for their appointment. This will bring the Northwest Territories Act into line with the Yukon Act, section 57 of which confers a similar power upon the governor in council.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, during the past summer, 1950, I took the opportunity of visiting the Northwest Territories and the Yukon. I spent as much time in both territories as I was able to do, and visited as many of the centres of population as possible as well as a number of outlying areas. I was quite impressed with the sense of responsibility of the people living in the north, and the great pride they are developing in the territories. Many people were asked about this matter of government, and I came to the conclusion that the time had come to extend some privileges to them in electing representatives to the territorial council. I believe that the feeling of the local people is that this is a step in the right direction. It is natural to expect that they feel the government should go the whole way just as quickly as it can. Undoubtedly there are people in the Northwest Territories who are of the opinion that there should be a fully elected council at the present time, and that this measure does not go far enough.
On the other hand I think the body of responsible opinion there is that, so long as the taxpayers of Canada are paying the great bulk of the expenditures in the territories, the process should be a gradual one. They recognize this as being about the right course of action for the present. The department, being responsible for the administration of the Northwest Territories, has tried to move in the direction of what one might term democracy just as quickly as possible. As any area has shown ability to administer its own affairs, appropriate responsibilities have been passed on to it. At the moment there is the Yellowknife administrative council which is a partially elected' council administering the affairs of the Yellowknife administrative district. There is also a fully elected school board in the Yellowknife district. In Hay River there is a partially elected council which administers its own affairs. Both these administrative districts do an excellent job of looking after their own affairs.

speechtext: It is true that any good administration tries to treat with the greatest equality the people for whom it is responsible. The Yukon territory has been set up as such, and is a responsibility of the federal government; and the federal government is doing its best to extend to the people who live in the Northwest Territories the same privileges as are available to people in other parts of Canada. I think perhaps the hon. member for Kootenay West is confusing local autonomy with the matter of general rights and privileges as Canadian citizens. There is no attempt to deny these people anything by virtue of the fact that they have not fully representative government.
