I am not satisfied with the minister's explanation as to why the appointed members of the council should decide who is going to vote in elections in
Northwest Territories Act the territory. It seems to me that we as a parliament here should be determining that matter instead of leaving it to some appointees of the government. It seems to me that would be the more democratic way to do it. As it stands, the qualifications for voting will be set by the appointees of the government who are civil servants of the government. It does not seem to me to be democratic to give to civil servants of the government the authority to determine who shall vote in an area of Canada. It seems to me that we should accept that responsibility as a parliament. Has the minister any explanation as to why we should give to appointees of the government, civil servants, the right to determine who shall vote and who shall not vote in a certain area of this country?

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR ELECTED REPRESENTATION IN TERRITORIAL GOVERNMENT AND APPOINTMENT OF JUDICIAL OFFICERS
speechtext: This is following the same pattern that has been followed in the Yukon Territory where the regulations governing voting are laid down by the commissioner in council. Under the Northwest Territories Act the government of the territories is assigned to the commissioner in council which passes ordinances which are tabled in the House of Commons. They are also subject to veto by the federal government. To that extent therefore the House of Commons here and the federal government have the final responsibility in any regulations that are laid down by the commissioner in council.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR ELECTED REPRESENTATION IN TERRITORIAL GOVERNMENT AND APPOINTMENT OF JUDICIAL OFFICERS
speechtext:
There are certain restrictions in the second clause. A person is not entitled to vote at an election unless he is a Canadian citizen, et cetera. In other words, there are certain things not within the discretion of the council and there are certain things which are within the discretion of the council. I should like to know what are the things that are within the discretion of the council, if these things are not; that is to say, that a person has to have attained the age of twenty-one, that he has to be a Canadian citizen, and that he has to be ordinarily resident in the territories for a period of at least twelve months immediately prior to the date of the election. If those things are not within the discretion of the council, what are the other qualifications of the voter which are within the discretion of such council? It is fairly well defined in this bill who shall be privileged to vote. Yet we are told that the final choice of the voter, if I may use that expression, is to be in the hands of the commissioner in council. I wonder what things are left. As a matter of fact, that is what worries me. I would rather see the

Northwest Territories Act whole thing left in the hands of the commissioner in council. But it describes these certain things and then we are left in the dark as to the certain other things that the council can decide. What are those things?

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR ELECTED REPRESENTATION IN TERRITORIAL GOVERNMENT AND APPOINTMENT OF JUDICIAL OFFICERS

It was felt that ,to follow the pattern of the Yukon Act, the section should phovide the council with the opportunity to make regulations as they see fit with respect to certain matters that have a bearing on who should vote and who should not vote.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR ELECTED REPRESENTATION IN TERRITORIAL GOVERNMENT AND APPOINTMENT OF JUDICIAL OFFICERS
speechtext: The minister has not made it plain to my satisfaction. I wish he could suggest what some of those certain matters might be. That is what I am concerned about. That is what I want to know.

speechtext:
The question is this: What
are some of the qualifications for a voter other than those mentioned in section 8A (2), namely, that a person is qualified to vote at an election if he is, (1) a Canadian citizen; (2) has attained th eage of 21 years; and (3) has been ordinarily resident in the territories for a period of not less than twelve months immediately prior to the date of the election.
If these are the grounds laid down by this act which permit a man to vote .then I ask the minister what are the other grounds upon which the commissioner in council may
IMr. Knight.]
refuse someone in that territory the right to vote? The bill says:
Subject to subsection two, the commissioner in council may prescribe the qualifications of those entitled to vote at an election of members to the council.
Then in the next clause the act itself prescribes those qualifications, but we are left in the dark as to what are the qualifications, or the lack of qualifications, upon which the commissioner in council may refuse such a vote. The thing is a deep, dark mystery. What are the qualifications that should leave the selection of the voters in the hands of the commissioner in council? May I say that, so far as I am concerned, I would not be prepared to leave the commissioner in council any discretion as to who shall or who shall not have a vote, but that this parliament should lay down the qualifications in this legislation, as an attempt has been made to lay down certain qualifications of a voter in clause 2. I hope I have made it clear.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR ELECTED REPRESENTATION IN TERRITORIAL GOVERNMENT AND APPOINTMENT OF JUDICIAL OFFICERS
speechtext:
My constituency goes right up to the Northwest Territories. I want fully to endorse the statement made by the hon. member for Yukon-Mackenzie River that everyone should be elected even though it is the Northwest Territories that are mentioned now. I fully endorse that democratic system of doing things, no matter how sparse is the population.
I should like to say this. Some years ago great men in eastern Canada looked at the west and they said, in developing the west we must have a railroad. It is time that the people of Canada looked to the north, and it is time that the northwest of Canada had a

railroad. The amount of wealth that is in that north country can only be handled by railroad facilities. There has been some talk, and I understand action is going on now, to put a railroad up to Lynn lake. That could go from Lynn lake north of Reindeer lake, north to Athabaska and up to Fort Smith to tap the minerals south of Great Slave lake and out to Prince George. In this part of the world that sounds like something ridiculous, but I want to assure you that it is not ridiculous. It is time that the Northwest Territories were tapped. It is time that we found out what wealth is in that country, and it is time that the people of Canada began to realize what advantages there are up in that country. On that railroad it is suggested that you could find everything from agriculture, mining and fishing right down to the part of civilization that has now made a great name for itself in the north, namely, Flin Flon. You could start from Flin Flon and do as I suggest and even if we do not get anything else done we should have a survey made.
I should like to point out to the minister that if he wants to make the Northwest Territories the first thing he has to do is to see that they get transportation in there.

speechtext: I still do not see why we should leave this matter of the qualifications of voters to a non-elected body. Has the minister any objections to the qualifications that we have in the Dominion Elections Act applying to voters in the Yukon? It seems to me that they apply to them with regard to dominion elections, and the same qualifications might apply in the Northwest Territories. There you have something that we have agreed on. We have agreed on certain qualifications for voters in the dominion elections, and I can see no reason why those qualifications should not apply in the elections in the Northwest Territories for councillors. Has the minister any objection to the qualifications that we have in the Dominion Elections Act being applied?

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR ELECTED REPRESENTATION IN TERRITORIAL GOVERNMENT AND APPOINTMENT OF JUDICIAL OFFICERS
speechtext:
The government of the Northwest Territories by the commissioner and his council is somewhat analogous to the government of a province by the provincial premier and his government. The provincial legislative body can give consideration to matters of voting in provincial elections, and following the pattern of the Yukon, where roughly a similar form of government exists, voting qualifications are fixed by the commissioner in council. Since the commissioner and his council are responsible for the
Northwest Territories Act administration of the territories, I think that matters other than those defined by this act should be left to their determination.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR ELECTED REPRESENTATION IN TERRITORIAL GOVERNMENT AND APPOINTMENT OF JUDICIAL OFFICERS
speechtext:
I am afraid the minister has given away his whole case now. I think his explanation has only led him into deep water. He says that the government of the Northwest Territories by the council is analogous to the government of a province by the premier and his government. The minister completely overlooked the fact that the provincial legislatures are sovereign, and it is the legislatures of the provinces that lay down these rules as to qualifications of voters.
The governing body responsible for the government of the Northwest Territories is this parliament, and this parliament simply appoints administrators in that area and a council with certain defined and delegated powers-because remember these are delegated powers, nothing more-but the rights of the provinces are not delegated. They are sovereign legislatures deriving their powers under the constitution. For the minister to say that because the provinces with their sovereign legislatures have the right to prescribe the qualifications of their voters, a body appointed under federal authority by the government should have that same power, seems to me to be just reducing the whole matter to a hopeless absurdity.
The minister has completely-and I regret to say this-completely misunderstood the matter. It is parliament that is responsible for the administration of the Northwest Territories. And if parliament is going to delegate some of its governing functions to a council up there, and is going to say that part of the governing body is to be elected, and then goes on to specify some of the qualifications of the voters, then surely it would be a most extraordinary thing for parliament to stop there after defining some of the qualifications of voters, and then leave it to others who enjoy the delegated powers from parliament, through the government, to specify the qualifications, or at least some of the qualifications of voters.
If it is possible for parliament to specify some of those qualifications, then certainly parliament can specify all. It would be an extraordinary thing to give to these persons possessing powers delegated by parliament the right to specify qualifications for voters who are going to vote on candidates for election to that governing body up there. That would be a most extraordinary thing. I suggest the minister should reconsider the whole matter.

Northwest Territories Act
If parliament can specify some of these qualifications, then certainly parliament is competent to specify all of them; and it would be a dangerous departure from principle if parliament did not go on to specify them all.

Mr. Chairman, I think the minister is moving along historical lines. For some years provinces have been set up in the western part of this land. It is not long ago that the people of the Northwest Territories were being taxed, although they did not have representation at all. I am referring to that part of the Northwest Territories now under discussion.
This is a step forward. It is a step that was taken in connection with Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta. That is a matter of record

here. But at the same time I believe the people in the Northwest Territories will very soon desire autonomy and absolute control of their own affairs, just as those other provinces have desired in times gone by. This is a step in that direction.
I believe hon. members would agree that autonomy would be a splendid thing for the Northwest Territories at such time as the population has been somewhat increased, transportation facilities made available, an immigration policy initiated, and the course followed which was the pattern in connection with Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta.

What the government is attempting to do is to extend to the body

designated to administer the affairs of the Northwest Territories more responsibilities, by giving it elected representation.
We are seeking to put into its hands more authority to run its own affairs, and to determine how its affairs should be run. By this amendment we would be taking away from the council of the Northwest Territories certain powers which we think it right and proper that it should have. subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR ELECTED REPRESENTATION IN TERRITORIAL GOVERNMENT AND APPOINTMENT OF JUDICIAL OFFICERS

I disagree with what the minister has just said because, in effect, this is what he is doing: He is trying to do by the back-door method something which apparently he is not prepared to do in the house, namely to define the qualification of voters. He appoints the majority on the commission, and therefore he can lay down the control of qualifications. If we are going to control qualifications, then we should do it by a method which is apparent to everyone, instead of doing it by controlling the number of appointed representatives on the commission, and therefore by that method say who shall be qualified to vote. If a majority of them were elected, then there would be some justification for the minister's argument, but when a majority are appointed I cannot see where his argument holds at all.

speechtext:
The minister and the government have not accepted the last suggested amendment to section 3. There is a population of 16,000 and the revenue has been increasing in that area. Over a long period of years the people have shown a lot of ability, especially in voting. For many years they sent the Hon. George Black here and now they have sent the present member for Yukon-Mackenzie River. If these two men are any example-and I think they are -of the calibre of people they have in that country, they certainly are capable of controlling their own vote. The first clause says that there shall be a council of the Northwest Territories consisting of eight members, three of whom shall be elected to represent electoral districts and five of whom shall be appointed by the governor in council. Three out of eight does not give these people very much representation. The minister also said that there were three electoral districts, Mackenzie, Keewatin and Franklin, and they are governed by the commissioner and deputy commissioner. Therefore there are really
Northwest Territories Act ten on that council, and only three representatives out of the ten are to be elected.
I think the government should give these people more of a lead than that because it does not seem that they have any representation whatsoever. I move as follows:
That the word "three" in line four and the word "five" in the fifth line be deleted, and that there shall be substituted the word "six" in the fourth line and the word "two" in the fifth line.
The section will then read as follows:
There shall be a council in the Northwest Territories consisting of eight numbers, six of whom shall be elected to represent electoral districts, and two of whom shall be appointed by the governor in council.
